title: Real-world debugging scenarios
blurb: "It works locally but not in production." Scenario questions where the interviewer wants to hear your reasoning, not a memorised fact.

questions.q: Right after a deploy, your API returns 401 for every request. The logs show the Authorization header arriving and the error 'signature validation failed'. Most likely cause?
choices: The server clock is a few minutes behind, so every incoming token looks as if it has expired
A reverse proxy is stripping the Authorization header before it reaches the app
The signing key or issuer configured in production differs from the one issuing tokens
A CORS preflight is failing, so the browser sends the request without its credentials
questions.why: A signature failure means the token arrived but was checked against a different key, which points at environment configuration. Clock skew produces a lifetime error instead, and the logs already rule out a stripped header. 'What differs about this environment?' is almost always the right first question.
questions.asked: Tests whether you read the evidence in the logs before guessing; the strong answer names the error text as the clue.

questions.q: A page loads in 200 ms locally and 8 seconds in production with the same code. Most likely cause?
choices: Production hardware is slower, so the same code needs a larger instance size
Data volume: a query that is fine over 50 local rows scans millions in production
The production bundle was shipped unminified, so the browser spends seconds parsing it
The CDN in front of production is missing, so every asset crosses the ocean
questions.why: Local databases are tiny and warm. Turn on query logging, run EXPLAIN on the slow query and look for a sequential scan or an N+1. Hardware differences explain tens of percent, not a 40-fold slowdown.
questions.asked: One of the best scenario questions there is: it separates guessers from people who instrument.

questions.q: Users report 'sometimes my changes don't save', and you cannot reproduce it. What is a likely explanation?
choices: The database silently drops writes while its connection pool is briefly exhausted
The browser caches the POST responses, so some of the saves never reach the server at all
A race: overlapping requests cause a lost update, or a slow response overwrites newer state
The ORM batches writes and flushes them only when the connection pool recycles
questions.why: Intermittent means timing. Look for a missing await, a fetch race, an update with no version check, or an optimistic update that never reconciled. An exhausted pool throws an error; it does not drop writes silently. Add a correlation id and log the write path.
questions.asked: Checks whether "intermittent" makes you think of concurrency before blaming the database or the user.

questions.q: Memory grows steadily until the service is killed and restarted. Where do you look?
choices: Unbounded caches, listeners never removed, or references piling up in a long-lived object
The garbage collector is misconfigured and needs a larger heap limit to keep up
Request volume: memory rises with traffic and is released only when traffic drops
The Docker image is too large, and all of its layers are loaded into the process memory
questions.why: A cache with no eviction is the classic: a memory leak with a nice name. A bigger heap only delays the kill. Take two heap snapshots under load and compare what grew between them.
questions.asked: A production-experience question; naming heap snapshots and a concrete leak pattern is what separates a real answer.

questions.q: The frontend gets a CORS error calling your API. Where is the fix?
choices: In the fetch call: set `mode: 'no-cors'` so the browser lets the response through
On the API: return the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers, including on OPTIONS
In the fetch call: add an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to the outgoing request
In DNS: point the API and frontend at the same IP address so they share an origin
questions.why: Only the server can grant the browser permission. `no-cors` gives you an opaque response you cannot read, and Allow-* headers on the request are ignored. An origin is scheme, host and port, not an IP. Check that OPTIONS is routed and the origin is listed exactly.
questions.asked: The most common frontend/backend integration failure, and the wrong answer, 'mode: no-cors', is very common.

questions.q: A request hangs forever instead of returning an error. What is the usual cause?
choices: The server ran out of memory, so the request is parked until memory frees up
The client cancelled it, and the server holds the socket open until a restart
A CORS failure, which leaves the request pending instead of returning an error
A promise that never settles, or an upstream call made with no timeout at all
questions.why: Every outbound call needs a timeout. Without one, a slow dependency ties up connections until the whole service looks down. Out-of-memory crashes the process, and CORS failures reject immediately; neither hangs.
questions.asked: The follow-up is "where would you put timeouts?"; the strong answer says on every outbound call.

questions.q: Re-running CI on a commit that passed last week now fails, and nothing in the repository changed. Most likely reason?
choices: The CI cache expired, and a build cannot pass until the cache is warm again
A dependency, base image or CI action resolved to a newer version because nothing pinned it
Git re-hashed the commit after a force-push to another branch, so CI now checks out different code
The pipeline file is read from main rather than the commit, so any main change breaks it
questions.why: 'Nothing changed' usually means nothing you changed. Check whether CI runs `npm ci`, whether a base image tag moved, or whether an action is pinned to a floating tag. A commit's hash is its content, so it cannot be re-hashed.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know every place a build pulls in something that is not in the commit.

questions.q: A React list uses `item.id` as the key, but after an import two items share an id. What symptom do you expect?
choices: A render error that unmounts the list until the duplicate item is removed from state
Nothing visible; React falls back to index keys for the two items that collide
A duplicate-key warning, and rows that get duplicated or dropped when the list updates
Each of the two rows shows the first item's data, while updates to either still apply correctly
questions.why: React logs "Encountered two children with the same key" and then its reconciliation is undefined for those children, so rows can be duplicated or omitted after an update. It does not throw and does not fall back to indices. Fix the data, not the key.
questions.asked: Checks that you connect a console warning to a data problem rather than silencing it.

questions.q: An endpoint is slow only for one large customer. What do you suspect?
choices: That customer's network is slow, which the server records as long response times
An unbounded query with no pagination, or no index covering the tenant column
Rate limiting is throttling them, because their many users share one API key
Their browser renders large tables slowly, which inflates the reported timings
questions.why: Slowness that scales with one tenant's data volume points at data access. Rate limiting returns 429 rather than slowing responses, and browser rendering does not show up in server timings. Put the tenant column in the index and cap result sizes.
questions.asked: A multi-tenant classic; the strong answer asks for the query plan with that tenant's id.

questions.q: Logs show the error but not which user or request it belongs to. What is missing?
choices: A higher log level, such as Debug, so every function call is recorded as well
More log statements around the failing code, each with the full request body
A log shipper that sends everything to one searchable place instead of local files
A correlation id on every log line for a request, passed on to downstream calls
questions.why: Without it you cannot pick one request's lines out of concurrent traffic. Centralising logs makes them searchable but does not link them. Generate the id at the edge, put it in the logging context, and return it in error responses so a user report maps to a query.
questions.asked: The strong answer mentions propagating the id to downstream services.

questions.q: A deploy succeeded, but some users see a blank page with a console error about a missing chunk. What happened?
choices: The CDN serves new HTML but old JavaScript, because its edge cache was never purged
The build skipped code splitting, so lazy routes were never emitted as files
Open tabs hold the old HTML, which references hashed bundles the deploy deleted
A CORS rule on the asset bucket blocks chunks loaded through dynamic import
questions.why: Only users with the app already open are hit: their old page asks for old chunk names that no longer exist. A skipped split or a CORS rule would break everyone, every time. Keep old assets for a grace period and reload the page on a chunk-load error.
questions.asked: A classic SPA deploy failure; people who have hit it mention keeping old assets around.

questions.q: A nightly background job has started running three times a night instead of once. Why?
choices: The cron expression fires hourly for three hours, because the hour field is a range
The job fails silently and the scheduler retries it twice before marking it done
Daylight saving makes the scheduler fire once for each offset it has seen
The app now runs three instances, and each has its own in-process scheduler
questions.why: An in-process scheduler scales with your replicas. Elect a leader, take a distributed lock, or move scheduling to something that runs the job once. A retry or a cron mistake would not line up with a change in instance count.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about what happens to in-process state when you scale out.

questions.q: The same order appears twice after a user double-clicked Submit. What prevents it even for retries and direct API calls?
choices: Debouncing the click handler so a second click within 300 ms is ignored
An idempotency key or unique constraint, so the server accepts it only once
Disabling the button while the request is in flight, so it cannot be clicked
Checking in the handler for an identical order before inserting the new one
questions.why: Client fixes help but a network retry or a direct API call bypasses them. A check-then-insert in the handler races with itself; only a constraint or a stored idempotency key makes 'this happens once' true on the server.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know which side of the wire can actually guarantee "once".

questions.q: Dates are one day off for some users. What is the likely cause?
choices: A leap-year bug in the date library that shifts dates after 29 February by one day
Time zones: a UTC instant shown in local time, or a date-only value read as UTC midnight
The database server sits in another region and stores dates in its own local zone
JSON cannot represent dates, so they can lose a day when serialised to text and parsed back
questions.why: `new Date('2026-03-01')` is parsed as UTC midnight, which is the previous evening west of Greenwich. Store instants in UTC and calendar dates as plain dates; they are genuinely different types. 'Some users' is the clue that points at location.
questions.asked: Everyone has shipped this bug; the strong answer separates instants from calendar dates.

questions.q: You get a 502 from your API behind a load balancer. What does that usually mean?
choices: The client sent a malformed request that the load balancer could not route
The DNS record for the API points at an old address with no server behind it
The TLS certificate on the load balancer expired, so the browser refused to connect to it
The app behind the proxy did not answer properly: crashed, not listening, or a bad reply
questions.why: 502 is the proxy saying its upstream failed. Check the app's logs and health first: common causes are a crash on startup, binding to localhost instead of 0.0.0.0, or a response the proxy could not parse; an upstream that is merely slow usually shows as 504 instead. A malformed request is a 400, and a bad certificate never reaches HTTP at all.
questions.asked: Tests whether you read a status code as "which hop failed", which is how you debug through proxies.

questions.q: How do you approach a bug you cannot reproduce?
choices: Find what the failing cases share, form a hypothesis, and add logging to test it
Rewrite the affected component cleanly, since the bug is likely in the messy parts
Wrap the suspect code in try/catch and log a warning so users stop seeing errors
Ask QA to try every browser until someone finds the steps that trigger the bug
questions.why: Ask what is different about the failing cases: user, tenant, browser, time, data shape. Then instrument to confirm or kill a hypothesis. Rewriting or swallowing the error changes the symptom without explaining it.
questions.asked: An open question where the interviewer is listening for a systematic process.

questions.q: A test suite passes but the same code fails in production. What is the most useful reflection?
choices: Coverage was too low; raising the threshold to 90% would have caught the case
The tests stopped at a boundary: real data, config, concurrency or a dependency
The tests were flaky, so a failing run was probably retried until it passed
Unit tests cannot catch production bugs, so the team should add manual QA
questions.why: Heavily mocked tests verify your assumptions, not reality. Ask "what kind of test would have caught this?"; the answer is often an integration test. Coverage measures executed lines, so a higher number would not have covered a boundary you mocked away.
questions.asked: Tests whether you learn from an escaped bug or only fix it.

questions.q: Your service degrades under load: response times climb until requests time out. First hypothesis?
choices: A bounded resource is exhausted, such as a connection or thread pool, and requests queue
The CPU is too slow for the workload, so each request takes longer as users arrive
The database needs more RAM, because each new user adds rows it holds in memory
The garbage collector runs more often under load, which on its own doubles every response time
questions.why: Latency climbing while throughput flattens is a queueing signature. Find what is saturated: pool metrics, upstream latency, GC pauses. Adding instances without fixing the bottleneck can make it worse by adding contention on the same database.
questions.asked: A production-experience signal; the strong answer mentions pool metrics before hardware.

questions.q: A user says 'the site is broken' with no other detail. What do you ask for?
choices: Whether they tried another browser, and to clear their cache before reporting
What they did, expected and saw, when it happened, and any error id on screen
A screen recording, since written descriptions from users are rarely usable
A formal ticket, so the report can be triaged in the next sprint planning
questions.why: Steps, expectation, outcome and a timestamp let you find the request in the logs. That is also why a visible correlation id on error pages is worth the small effort. A recording helps sometimes, but it still lacks the time and id you need to search.
questions.asked: Checks whether you can turn a vague report into something searchable.

questions.q: You have found and fixed the cause of an outage. What comes next?
choices: A meeting to agree who caused it and what training that person now needs
A new alert for this exact error, so the same failure pages someone next time
A blameless write-up: what happened, why, and what change stops the whole class
Closing the incident once the fix is live, since the cause is now understood
questions.why: The valuable output is the systemic change (a test, a guardrail, an alert, a process), not the individual patch. An alert for the exact error helps but does not stop the class recurring, and blame makes people hide the next incident.
questions.asked: A maturity question. 'Blameless' is the word worth using.

questions.q: The browser shows stale data after an update, but `curl` against the API returns the new value. Why?
choices: The user's session holds a snapshot of the data taken when they logged in
A cache is serving the old response: browser, service worker, CDN or query cache
The browser speaks HTTP/1.1 while curl uses HTTP/2, which always fetches newer data
A CORS rule blocks the fresh response, so the browser falls back to an old one
questions.why: Work outward from the client: devtools with cache disabled, then Cache-Control headers, the CDN, and whether the frontend query cache was invalidated after the mutation. Protocol version does not change which data a server returns.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know how many caches sit between a user and your database.

questions.q: Production is down for all users. What is the first thing to do?
choices: Find the root cause before touching anything, so the evidence is not destroyed
Restore service by rolling back or mitigating, then investigate the cause
Write a failing test that reproduces the outage, then fix forward against it
Email every stakeholder with an impact estimate before anyone changes anything
questions.why: Recovery and diagnosis are separate goals. Rolling back to a known-good version stops the damage and buys time to investigate properly. The regression test belongs to the fix that follows, once users are served again.
questions.asked: Checks whether you put users before curiosity; the strong answer also mentions keeping logs for the investigation.

questions.q: A build works on your laptop but fails in CI with a syntax error inside a dependency. What do you check first?
choices: Whether your laptop has a newer Git that checks files out with other line endings
Whether CI runs a different Node or .NET version, and pin it in `.nvmrc` or `global.json`
Whether the CI runner has less memory, since the parser reports syntax errors when it runs out
Whether the dependency came from a mirror that serves corrupted package archives
questions.why: A syntax error in someone else's code usually means that code targets a newer runtime than the one executing it. Pin the version in the repo (`.nvmrc`, `engines`, `global.json`) and have CI read it. Low memory crashes the process; it does not produce a syntax error.
questions.asked: A junior check that you treat the runtime version as part of the code.

questions.q: A production error's stack trace points at `main.4f9a1c.js:1:48213`. What turns it into a readable file and line?
choices: Rebuilding the app locally in development mode and matching the column number
Turning off minification in production so that future stack traces are readable
Running the bundle through a code formatter, which restores the original names
The source map from that exact build, uploaded to your error tracker or kept private
questions.why: A source map maps minified positions back to original files and names, but only for the build that produced it, so store maps per release. A formatter adds line breaks but cannot recover renamed variables, and a fresh local build has different offsets.
questions.asked: Checks whether you have debugged a real production frontend rather than only a dev server.

questions.q: A checkout request takes 3 s and calls four internal services. What shows you which hop is slow?
choices: Each service's CPU graph, since the slow one will show the highest CPU usage
A load test of each service alone, since the slowest in isolation is the culprit
Distributed tracing: one trace id, with a timed span for every service call
The load balancer's access log, which records time spent inside each service
questions.why: A trace follows one request across services and shows each span's duration, including time spent waiting on another call. A slow hop is often waiting on I/O with low CPU, and a service that is fast in isolation can still be slow under the real call pattern.
questions.asked: Leads into OpenTelemetry and context propagation; people who have used traces describe spans, not just logs.

questions.q: For a request-serving API, what do the RED metrics track?
choices: Reads, Egress bytes and Disk usage for each host behind the API
Rate of requests, Errors, and Duration of those requests
Retries, Exceptions and Dependency calls made for each request
Requests per user, Error budget left, and Deployment frequency
questions.why: RED describes a service from its callers' view: how much traffic, how much fails, how slow. Its sibling USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) describes resources such as CPU, disks and pools. Together they tell you whether users hurt and which resource is to blame.
questions.asked: Tests whether you would know what to put on a service dashboard on day one.

questions.q: Your team ignores alerts because most fire on CPU spikes users never notice. Which change best cuts the noise without missing real outages?
choices: Raise every CPU threshold from 80% to 95%, so only extreme spikes page anyone
Page on SLO burn rate, such as errors eating the monthly budget too quickly
Send all alerts to a shared channel instead of paging, and review it each morning
Alert on every error log line, so no failure goes unseen by the on-call engineer
questions.why: Alert on symptoms users feel, measured against an objective, and keep cause metrics such as CPU for dashboards. A higher CPU threshold still pages on spikes nobody feels and can miss an outage with low CPU; a morning review is not paging at all.
questions.asked: An on-call maturity question; the strong answer distinguishes symptom alerts from cause dashboards.

questions.q: Overnight, every browser shows a security warning for your site, though nothing was deployed. Most likely cause?
choices: A browser update dropped support for HTTP/1.1, which your server still speaks
The DNS provider rotated your IP address, so the domain now points elsewhere
The server's clock drifted, so it now rejects every client's encryption keys
The TLS certificate expired because its renewal did not run or quietly failed
questions.why: Certificates expire on a fixed date whether or not you deploy, and automated renewal fails silently more often than people expect. Monitor expiry dates and alert weeks ahead. Browsers still support HTTP/1.1, and a moved IP gives a connection error, not a certificate warning.
questions.asked: Almost every team has had this outage once; the strong answer adds expiry monitoring.

questions.q: A service that ran fine for months now fails every write with 'No space left on device'. What is the classic cause?
choices: Log files growing with no rotation or retention until they filled the disk
The database reached its maximum row count and reports it as a full disk
Memory ran out, and the operating system reports swap exhaustion as a disk error
Too many open connections, each of which reserves a block of disk space
questions.why: Months of steady growth that suddenly bites is the signature of unrotated logs (or temp files). Configure rotation and retention, ship logs off the box, and alert on disk usage before it reaches 100%.
questions.asked: A junior operations check; the follow-up is "how would you have seen it coming?".

questions.q: Uploads under 1 MB work, but larger ones fail immediately with HTTP 413. What is happening?
choices: The upload timed out on a slow connection, and servers report timeouts as 413
The file type is not allowed, and 413 is the status for unsupported media
A request-body size limit in the proxy or the app rejects it before your code runs
The user's storage quota is full, so the server refuses anything over the rest
questions.why: 413 Content Too Large means some layer refused the body by size. Nginx, for example, defaults `client_max_body_size` to 1 MB, and frameworks have their own limits, so check every hop. Unsupported media is 415 and a timeout is 408 or 504.
questions.asked: Tests whether you read a status code precisely and think about every layer between browser and handler.

questions.q: Under load, a few writes fail with SQL Server error 1205, 'chosen as the deadlock victim'. What does it mean for the failed request?
choices: The database ran out of connections and will refuse all writes until restarted
Its transaction was killed and rolled back to break a lock cycle, and is safe to retry
The transaction partly committed before failing, so the rows it touched must be repaired by hand
The query timed out waiting on a slow scan, so adding an index resolves it
questions.why: The engine detected two transactions waiting on each other and rolled one back entirely, so retrying it is safe. Capture the deadlock graph (or Postgres's "deadlock detected" log detail) to see which statements collided. Nothing is left half-written.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know deadlocks are a normal event to retry and log, not data corruption.

questions.q: In this docker-compose setup the API cannot connect to the database. Why?
questions.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      DB_HOST: localhost
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
choices: Compose puts each service on its own network unless you declare a shared one
Inside the api container, `localhost` is that container; use the service name `db`
Postgres listens on 5432 only when a `ports:` mapping publishes it to the host
The postgres image only accepts connections when `DB_HOST` is set to `0.0.0.0`
questions.why: Each container has its own network namespace, so `localhost` means the api container. Compose puts all services on one default network with DNS by service name, so `DB_HOST: db` works. `ports:` only matters for reaching the container from the host.
questions.asked: The first thing everyone hits with Compose; explaining why shows you understand container networking.

questions.q: Production quietly used a default value because an environment variable name had a typo. What prevents this class of bug?
choices: Give every setting a sensible default so the app always starts, even if misnamed
Log each config value at debug level so the wrong one can be traced afterwards
Validate required config at startup and refuse to boot when a value is missing
Keep all settings in one committed JSON file instead of environment variables
questions.why: Fail fast: a missing required setting should stop the deploy, where it is cheap, not surface weeks later as odd behaviour. Defaults for required production values are exactly what hid the typo. Schema validation of config at boot (for example zod, or .NET `ValidateOnStart`) does this.
questions.asked: Checks whether you prefer loud failures to silent ones, which is most of production hygiene.

questions.q: You roll back a bad release, but errors continue. The release had run a migration that dropped a column. Why did rolling back not help?
choices: The rollback also reverted the database, losing every row written since the release
The migration only goes forward, so the old code now runs against a schema missing its column
Caches still hold the new version's responses, and they expire only at the next deploy
Rollbacks swap images node by node, so errors carry on until every last node has been restarted
questions.why: Rolling back code does not roll back schema, and a dropped column cannot come back by redeploying. That is why destructive migrations ship in a later release than the code that stops using the column, so rollback always stays possible.
questions.asked: Connects deployment to migrations; people who have been bitten describe expand/contract unprompted.

questions.q: In a Node or ASP.NET Core service, a bug disappears when you add logging around it and returns when you remove the logging. What does that point to?
choices: A compiler optimisation that the logging call disables by marking a variable as used
A memory leak; the logging allocates enough to trigger a collection that hides it
A caching bug; reading the value for the log line refreshes a stale cache entry
A timing-dependent race; the logging's delay changes the order things run in
questions.why: Logging adds I/O and delay, which reorders concurrent work, so the race stops showing. Look for shared state touched by overlapping async operations. Neither V8 nor the .NET JIT changes program meaning because a variable is logged.
questions.asked: A "have you really debugged concurrency?" question; naming the observer effect is the signal.

questions.q: A service sits at 100% CPU under normal traffic while its memory stays flat. What do you capture first?
choices: A CPU profile or flame graph under load, to see which functions burn the time
Two heap snapshots a while apart, to see which objects are accumulating
A network capture, to see whether responses are slow to leave the host
A GC trace, since full CPU in a managed runtime is almost always the collector
questions.why: Match the tool to the symptom: CPU saturation calls for a CPU profile, growing memory for heap snapshots. With memory flat, garbage collection is unlikely to be the main cost, and a network capture says nothing about where CPU goes.
questions.asked: Tests whether you pick a profiler from the symptom rather than reaching for the one tool you know.

questions.q: A nightly cleanup job stopped running two months ago and nobody noticed until the disk filled. Which monitoring change catches this class of failure?
choices: Raise the log level of the job to Debug so that each step it takes is written out in full for later reading
Alert whenever the job logs an error, since a job that has stopped will keep producing error lines
Add a retry so that a job that fails at 02:00 runs again at 03:00 and 04:00 before it finally gives up
Alert when the job's success signal is missing past its schedule, not only when it reports a failure
questions.why: A job that never starts logs nothing, so error alerts and retries stay silent; only the absence of a heartbeat (a dead man's switch, or an alert on the age of the last success) turns 'it did not run' into a page. More log detail helps once someone is looking, but nobody was. Retries help a job that runs and fails; this one was never scheduled, perhaps because the instance that owned the cron was replaced.
questions.asked: An on-call classic that separates alerting on errors from alerting on missing expected events; 'dead man's switch' is the phrase interviewers hope for.

questions.q: In React 19 development, an effect that posts an analytics event fires twice on mount, but only once in production. What is going on?
choices: The component is rendered by two different parents, so it mounts twice everywhere
Strict Mode remounts components once in development to expose effects missing cleanup
The dev server sends each network request twice to warm the HTTP cache for the page
React 19 batches effects differently in development and replays the last one it ran
questions.why: Strict Mode deliberately runs an extra setup-cleanup cycle in development so effects without proper cleanup show their bug. The fix is idempotent effects or cleanup, not removing Strict Mode; production mounts once.
questions.asked: A very common 'bug' report from juniors; the strong answer explains why React does it on purpose.

questions.q: A React 19 counter increments once per second, but the displayed value sticks at 1. What is the bug?
choices: `setInterval` is throttled in React components, so it only fires the once
The cleanup runs immediately after setup, so the interval is cleared again each second
The interval callback closes over `count` from the first render, which is always 0
`useState` setters ignore values that are computed from the previous state
questions.why: With an empty dependency array the effect runs once, and its callback keeps seeing `count === 0`, so it sets 1 forever. Use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` so the callback no longer depends on a stale closure.
questions.asked: Stale closures are the most common hooks bug in real code; the updater-function fix is what interviewers want.

questions.q: A Next.js or React SSR page logs 'Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client'. The component shows `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()`. Why?
choices: Server and browser render at different moments, often in different zones and locales
`toLocaleTimeString` is not available in Node, so the server renders an empty string
Hydration fails whenever a component uses any built-in JavaScript Date method
The browser's clock is ahead of the server's, and React refuses to hydrate future times
questions.why: Hydration expects the client's first render to produce the same markup as the server's. Times, random values and locale-dependent formatting differ, so render them only after mount (in an effect) or pass the server's value down as data.
questions.asked: Hydration errors are a daily SSR headache; strong answers list the usual non-deterministic sources.

questions.q: After a deploy, some users keep seeing the old version of your PWA even after refreshing. The app registers a service worker. What is the likely cause?
choices: The CDN is ignoring your cache headers, so it serves the old version forever
Browsers keep a separate copy of each site's JavaScript for every open tab
The new build failed to deploy for users in some regions of the world
The old service worker serves cached assets until the new one takes control
questions.why: A new service worker installs but waits until all tabs using the old one close; meanwhile the old worker keeps answering from its cache. Prompt users to reload on `waiting`, or use `skipWaiting` and `clients.claim` deliberately.
questions.asked: Shows you understand service worker lifecycle, which trips up almost every team that adds one.

questions.q: Your frontend on `app.example.com` calls `api.example.com` with `fetch`, but the session cookie is never sent. The server sets it with `SameSite=Lax`. What else is required?
choices: Setting `mode: 'no-cors'` on the fetch, so the browser skips the cookie check
Nothing, because cookies are always sent on every request to the same site
`credentials: 'include'` on the fetch, plus CORS allowing credentials for that origin
Renaming the cookie with a `__Host-` prefix so that it is shared across all subdomains
questions.why: Cross-origin fetches omit cookies unless you opt in with `credentials: 'include'`, and the API must reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and an explicit origin, not `*`. `__Host-` cookies are the opposite: locked to one host.
questions.asked: Cookie-plus-CORS bugs are extremely common in split frontend and API deployments.

questions.q: Login works on `http://localhost` but on the HTTPS staging site the browser drops the auth cookie. It is set with `SameSite=None` but without `Secure`. Why?
choices: Browsers reject `SameSite=None` cookies that are not also marked `Secure`
Staging sites are treated as third-party domains, which block all cookies
`SameSite=None` only works on localhost, as a development convenience
HTTPS strips all cookie attributes, so the cookie arrives with no name
questions.why: Modern browsers require `Secure` on any `SameSite=None` cookie and silently discard it otherwise; the DevTools cookie panel shows a warning. Localhost gets special treatment, which is why it 'works on my machine'.
questions.asked: Browsers log it quietly, so candidates who have debugged cookie issues know to look in the Application panel.

questions.q: After adding a Content-Security-Policy header, your analytics script and an inline `onclick` handler stop working. What does the console most likely show?
choices: A CORS error, because CSP and CORS are the same browser mechanism
A 403 from the server, since CSP blocks the requests on the server side before sending
Refused to load or execute them because they violate the policy's `script-src`
A mixed-content warning, since CSP forces all scripts onto plain HTTP
questions.why: CSP is enforced by the browser: scripts from unlisted origins and inline handlers are blocked unless allowed, and each violation is logged. Add the analytics origin, move inline handlers into scripts, or use nonces; roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.
questions.asked: Shows you can adopt CSP without breaking the site; report-only mode is the strong detail.

questions.q: Your HTTPS page loads an image from `http://cdn.example.com/logo.png`, and it does not appear. What is happening?
choices: The CDN rejects requests that come from pages served over HTTPS connections
Images over HTTP are allowed, but the browser lazy-loads them only once the user scrolls
The image is too large, so the browser cancels it on a secure connection
Mixed content: the browser upgrades or blocks HTTP subresources on HTTPS pages
questions.why: Browsers block active mixed content and now auto-upgrade or block passive content such as images, so an HTTP URL on an HTTPS page fails if the host has no HTTPS. Serve every asset over HTTPS or use protocol-relative config from the environment.
questions.asked: A common bug after moving a site to HTTPS; easy points if you name it.

questions.q: The React app reads `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. You change the variable in the hosting dashboard and restart, but the app still calls the old URL. Why?
choices: Vite reads environment variables only on the first request after each restart of the host
The value is inlined into the bundle at build time, so you must rebuild and redeploy
The browser caches environment variables in localStorage for up to a day
Dashboard variables apply only to server code and never to static sites
questions.why: Frontend bundlers replace `import.meta.env.*` with literal strings during the build, so the running bundle contains the old URL. Rebuild per environment, or load runtime config from a small `/config.json` fetched at start-up.
questions.asked: Build-time versus runtime config is a key distinction; strong answers offer the runtime-config alternative.

questions.q: A 'remember my draft' feature throws `QuotaExceededError` for a few users. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Those users' browsers do not support localStorage at all, so every call throws
localStorage is cleared on each reload, so writes fail when the page reloads
The origin's storage quota (about 5 MB) is full, or the browser restricts storage
The server rejected the draft, and the error is forwarded into the browser API
questions.why: localStorage has a small per-origin quota, and some privacy modes or embedded contexts restrict it further, so `setItem` can throw. Wrap access in try/catch, keep drafts small, and treat browser storage as a convenience that may fail.
questions.asked: Shows defensive thinking about browser APIs that 'always work' in development.

questions.q: Your API behind a TLS-terminating load balancer builds redirect URLs, and users land on `http://` links that redirect back to HTTPS in a loop. What is missing?
choices: A second TLS certificate on the app itself so it can serve HTTPS directly
A CDN between the balancer and the app to rewrite the scheme of each link it returns
An HSTS header on the balancer, which rewrites the app's generated URLs
Trusting `X-Forwarded-Proto` so the app knows the original request was HTTPS
questions.why: The app receives plain HTTP from the balancer and assumes the client did too. Enable forwarded-headers handling (`UseForwardedHeaders` in ASP.NET Core, `app.set('trust proxy', ...)` in Express) for the known proxy so scheme, host and client IP are correct.
questions.asked: A classic 'works locally, loops behind the proxy' bug; strong answers restrict trust to known proxies.

questions.q: Your Express app's rate limiter blocks everyone at once in production, though it works locally. The logs show every request coming from `10.0.3.17`. Why?
choices: The app sees the load balancer's IP, not the client's, because proxy trust is not set
A single attacker at `10.0.3.17` is flooding the API and triggering the limit
The rate limiter uses a shared counter that resets only once a day when run in production
Express converts IPv6 client addresses to one IPv4 address behind proxies
questions.why: Behind a proxy, the socket address is the proxy's, so all users share one rate-limit bucket. Configure `trust proxy` for your proxy hops so `req.ip` comes from `X-Forwarded-For`, without trusting arbitrary client-supplied headers.
questions.asked: Real production incident; strong answers mention not trusting `X-Forwarded-For` from anywhere.

questions.q: A third-party address-lookup API starts taking 30 seconds to respond. Soon your whole API is unresponsive, including endpoints that never call it. Why?
choices: Requests waiting on the slow dependency hold threads or connections until none are left
The third party is sending your API malicious payloads that crash every endpoint
Slow outbound calls make Node and .NET lower the priority of every other request
The load balancer marks your API unhealthy whenever a dependency is slow
questions.why: Without a short timeout, calls to the slow dependency pile up and exhaust shared resources (connection pools, thread pool, sockets), so unrelated requests queue too. Timeouts, a circuit breaker and a bulkhead (separate limit for that dependency) contain the failure.
questions.asked: Cascading failure from a slow dependency is a classic; strong answers name timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads.

questions.q: A report endpoint returns 504 Gateway Timeout after exactly 60 seconds, yet the app logs show the request completing successfully after 75 seconds. What happened?
choices: The app crashed at 60 seconds and restarted, then logged a different request
The browser has a 60-second limit and reported its own timeout as a 504 response code
The proxy's 60-second timeout fired first, so the app's late response was discarded
The database cancelled the query at 60 seconds but returned the rows anyway
questions.why: Each hop has its own timeout; the gateway gave up at 60 seconds and answered 504 while the app carried on. Either make the work faster, move it to a background job with 202 and polling, or align timeouts deliberately across the chain.
questions.asked: Tests layered-timeout reasoning; strong answers prefer an async job over raising every timeout.

questions.q: In Nginx access logs you see many HTTP 499 responses for your search endpoint. What does 499 mean?
choices: The upstream app returned an unknown error that Nginx could not classify
The request body was too large for the configured client buffer size
Nginx rejected the request because the rate limit for that client was hit
The client closed the connection before Nginx could send the response
questions.why: 499 is Nginx's own code for 'client closed request': the user navigated away, a fetch was aborted, or a caller's timeout fired. Many 499s on one endpoint usually mean it is too slow for its callers, or the frontend aborts superseded searches.
questions.asked: Reading proxy logs is a real skill; 499 is often misread as a server error.

questions.q: A WebSocket chat works locally but fails in production behind Nginx with a 400 or an immediate close. What is the most likely missing configuration?
choices: Forwarding the `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers and using HTTP/1.1 to the upstream
Enabling gzip for WebSocket frames, since uncompressed frames are rejected
Setting a CORS header, since WebSocket handshakes require a preflight request
Opening a separate TCP port for WebSockets, since they cannot share port 443 with HTTPS
questions.why: The WebSocket handshake is an HTTP/1.1 upgrade, and Nginx does not pass hop-by-hop `Upgrade`/`Connection` headers by default. Add `proxy_http_version 1.1` and set both headers, and raise idle timeouts for long-lived connections.
questions.asked: A standard real-time deployment bug; people who have shipped WebSockets know the two headers.

questions.q: One corporate user cannot reach your API: the browser reports `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`, but it works for everyone else and on SSL checkers. What is a likely cause?
choices: Your certificate expired only for users in that user's time zone
A corporate TLS-inspection proxy re-signs traffic with a CA their device lacks
The API rejects that user's IP, and the browser shows it as a certificate error
Your server sends a different certificate to every visitor for security reasons
questions.why: Middleboxes that intercept TLS present their own certificate, and if the device lacks the corporate root CA the browser rejects it. Checking the certificate issuer in the browser reveals it; the fix is on their network side.
questions.asked: Tests the ability to reason from 'only one user' to 'something on their path'.

questions.q: Browsers load your site fine, but a partner's Java or Node client fails with 'unable to verify the first certificate'. What should you check?
choices: That the partner's client supports HTTP/2, since HTTP/1.1 cannot verify certificates
That the certificate uses RSA, since elliptic-curve certificates fail in servers
That your server sends the full chain, including the intermediate certificate
That the certificate's expiry date is in the partner's local time zone
questions.why: Browsers often fetch or cache missing intermediates, masking a misconfigured server; many non-browser clients do not. Configure the server with the full chain file, and verify with `openssl s_client -showcerts` or an SSL checker.
questions.asked: A real integration bug that browser testing hides; strong answers mention testing with a CLI client.

questions.q: In production your ASP.NET Core API ignores settings in `appsettings.Production.json`. Locally, `appsettings.Development.json` works fine. What should you check first?
choices: That the JSON file is marked as an embedded resource so the runtime can read it
That `appsettings.json` has been deleted, since it overrides all other files
That the file name uses lowercase `production`, which Linux requires
That `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` really is `Production` and the file was published
questions.why: The environment-specific file is chosen by the environment name, which defaults to Production but is often overridden by a stray setting, and the file must be copied to the publish output. `appsettings.json` loads first and the environment file overrides it.
questions.asked: Environment-specific configuration is a basic .NET deployment skill interviewers check.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core app reads `ConnectionStrings:Default`. On the host you set the environment variable `ConnectionStrings:Default`, but Linux ignores it. What is the correct name?
choices: `CONNECTIONSTRINGS_DEFAULT`, since environment variables must be uppercase
`ConnectionStrings__Default`, using a double underscore for the section separator
`ConnectionStrings.Default`, using a dot, which Linux shells accept
`Default`, since connection strings are always read from the root of the configuration
questions.why: Colons are not portable in environment variable names, so the .NET configuration provider maps `__` to `:`. Names are case-insensitive for .NET, so uppercase is not required, but the separator is.
questions.asked: A small detail that causes real production outages; knowing it shows hands-on .NET deployment.

questions.q: A Node API works locally but crashes in production because `process.env.DATABASE_URL` is undefined. Locally, the value lives in a `.env` file. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The `.env` file is not deployed, and the variable was never set on the host itself
Node 24 ignores `.env` files unless the process runs as the root user
Environment variables are read-only in production, so the value is cleared
`process.env` only contains variables whose names are all lowercase
questions.why: `.env` files are a local convenience (loaded by dotenv or `node --env-file`) and should not ship; production must set variables on the host or in the platform's config. Validate required config at start-up so this fails loudly.
questions.asked: Tests whether config is understood as the environment's job; strong answers add start-up validation.

questions.q: Tests pass on your Mac and Windows machines but fail in the Linux CI with 'Cannot find module ./components/Header'. The file is `header.tsx`. Why?
choices: Linux cannot resolve `.tsx` extensions without an explicit loader flag
CI caches old files, so it is still looking at a `Header` file that has since been deleted
Linux filesystems are case-sensitive, so `Header` and `header` are different files
Module resolution on Linux requires every import path to be absolute
questions.why: macOS and Windows filesystems are case-insensitive by default, so a wrong-case import works locally. Linux containers and CI are case-sensitive. Fix the import; `forceConsistentCasingInFileNames` in tsconfig catches it earlier.
questions.asked: Very common cross-platform bug; mentioning the tsconfig flag is a strong detail.

questions.q: A shell script committed from Windows fails in a Linux container with `/bin/sh^M: bad interpreter`. What is wrong?
choices: The script is missing execute permission, and `^M` is the permission error code
The container's shell is too old to run scripts that were written on Windows
The script uses a Windows-only command that the shell prints as `^M`
The file has CRLF line endings, so the shebang line ends with a carriage return
questions.why: `^M` is a carriage return: the interpreter path became `/bin/sh\r`. Convert to LF and add a `.gitattributes` rule such as `*.sh text eol=lf` so git checks it out correctly on every machine.
questions.asked: Classic cross-platform trap; `.gitattributes` is the durable fix interviewers like.

questions.q: A Node script works when run from the project root but fails with ENOENT when a cron job runs it. It reads `fs.readFileSync('./data/config.json')`. Why?
choices: Relative paths resolve against the process's working directory, not the script's folder
Cron jobs cannot read JSON files unless they run with elevated permissions on the machine
`readFileSync` is disabled in non-interactive shells for safety reasons
The file is locked by the editor, which blocks reads from other processes
questions.why: `./` means `process.cwd()`, and cron starts in the home directory. Resolve paths relative to the module instead, for example `new URL('./data/config.json', import.meta.url)` or `path.join(import.meta.dirname, ...)`.
questions.asked: Working-directory bugs appear in every deployment; strong answers show the module-relative fix.

questions.q: A CI build fails with a type error inside a library, though you changed nothing. The lockfile is committed, but CI runs `npm install`. What is the fix?
choices: Delete the lockfile so that npm can pick the newest compatible versions on every run
Use `npm ci`, which installs exactly what the lockfile records and fails on mismatch
Add `--force` to `npm install` so it ignores type errors in dependencies
Pin the library with a caret range such as `^2.0.0` in `package.json`
questions.why: `npm install` may update the lockfile within `package.json` ranges, pulling a new release; `npm ci` installs the lockfile exactly and errors if it disagrees with `package.json`. A caret range allows the very drift that caused this.
questions.asked: Reproducible installs are a basic CI expectation; the npm ci answer is what interviewers listen for.

questions.q: The app builds locally on Node 24 but CI fails with `SyntaxError` on modern syntax, and the CI image uses Node 18. What durable fix stops this recurring?
choices: Transpile every dependency to ES5 so it runs on any version of Node
Remove the modern syntax from your code so it runs on older versions
Declare the version once (`.nvmrc` or `engines`) and have CI read it
Ask each developer to downgrade to Node 18 to match the CI image
questions.why: One source of truth for the runtime version, read by `actions/setup-node` (`node-version-file`), local tooling and the Dockerfile, keeps them aligned. Node 18 is also end-of-life, so CI should move up, not developers down.
questions.asked: Environment parity question; strong answers name a single version file.

questions.q: A test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs. Another test earlier in the run sets a module-level cache. What kind of bug is this?
choices: A flaky network dependency that only appears under heavy CI load
A timezone difference between the test runner and the code under test
A compiler bug that only appears when many test files are loaded
Order-dependent tests sharing state that one test leaves behind
questions.why: Shared mutable state (module singletons, globals, database rows) leaks between tests, so results depend on order. Reset state in `beforeEach`, isolate modules, or run with a random order to surface these early.
questions.asked: Test isolation is a core testing skill; interviewers like hearing about randomised order.

questions.q: A date-formatting test passes on your laptop in London and fails in CI. The expected string is `'24/09/2026'`. What is the most likely cause?
choices: CI runs in UTC and a different default locale, so the formatted output differs
The CI machine's clock is set to the wrong year, so the date is off
Date formatting in Node only works when a browser is present
The test framework rounds all dates to midnight UTC before comparing them with strings
questions.why: `toLocaleDateString()` without arguments uses the machine's locale and time zone, which differ between laptop and CI. Pass an explicit locale and `timeZone` in code and tests, or set `TZ` in the test environment.
questions.asked: Hidden environment dependencies in tests are common; strong answers make locale and zone explicit.

questions.q: Your Node image now runs as `USER node`. The app starts, but every upload fails with `EACCES: permission denied, open '/app/uploads/a.png'`. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The `node` user lacks write permission on `/app/uploads`, which was created as root
Uploads are blocked by the container runtime unless the port is published first
Node refuses to write files whose names end in an image extension without a flag
The filesystem inside every container image is mounted read-only by Docker itself
questions.why: Files and folders created earlier in the Dockerfile (by `COPY` or `RUN mkdir`) belong to root, so switching to a non-root user leaves them unwritable. Use `COPY --chown=node:node` or `chown` the directory, or better, write uploads to object storage or a mounted volume.
questions.asked: Running as non-root is best practice, and this is the bug it causes first; strong answers fix ownership rather than going back to root.

questions.q: Your API container starts and logs 'listening on localhost:3000', but the host cannot reach it on the published port. What is wrong?
choices: Port 3000 is reserved inside containers, so the app must use port 80
Containers cannot accept connections until a health check has passed
The app is bound to the container's loopback, so it must listen on `0.0.0.0`
The `-p 3000:3000` flag only works on Linux hosts, not under Docker on macOS or Windows
questions.why: Inside a container, `localhost` is the container's own loopback, which the published port cannot reach. Bind to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces), for example `app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0')` or `ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080`.
questions.asked: Probably the most common first container bug; quick recognition earns easy credit.

questions.q: A customer named `Zoë` appears as `ZoÃ«` in exported CSV files opened in Excel, while the web UI shows it correctly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The database column is too short, so the accented character was truncated on save
The file is UTF-8, but Excel is opening it with a legacy Windows encoding instead
The browser converted the name to ASCII before sending it to the export endpoint
The CSV writer escapes non-English letters as HTML entities by default in exports
questions.why: `Ã«` is what the two UTF-8 bytes for `ë` look like when decoded as Windows-1252: classic mojibake. The data is fine; write a UTF-8 BOM at the start of the CSV (Excel uses it to detect encoding) or offer an XLSX export.
questions.asked: Encoding bugs are everyday work with exports; recognising mojibake patterns speeds diagnosis.

questions.q: An order id from your API is `9007199254740993`, but the frontend shows and sends back `9007199254740992`. What happened?
choices: The API rounded the id to an even number before serialising the response
`JSON.parse` truncates every integer to 16 characters to protect memory
The id exceeds `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so it was parsed into the nearest double
The browser's fetch adds one to very large numbers to stop attackers enumerating ids
questions.why: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit doubles and only represent integers exactly up to 2^53 − 1; larger values snap to a neighbouring representable number. Send 64-bit ids (C# `long`, Postgres `bigint`) as strings in JSON.
questions.asked: A real integration bug between .NET or SQL bigints and JavaScript; the 'send as string' fix is the key.

questions.q: A daily 02:30 reminder job did not run on one Sunday in March and ran twice on one Sunday in October. The server uses local UK time. Why?
choices: The scheduler library has a leap-year bug that affects two Sundays a year
The database was in maintenance on those Sundays, and the job retried itself afterwards
Two servers were deployed on those weekends, and each one ran the job
Daylight saving: 02:30 did not exist on one day and occurred twice on the other
questions.why: When clocks jump forward, local times in the gap never happen; when they fall back, an hour repeats. Run schedulers in UTC, or pick a local time outside the transition window and make jobs idempotent.
questions.asked: Time zones and DST produce memorable bugs; strong answers say 'schedule in UTC, make jobs idempotent'.

questions.q: A price input accepts `1,50` from a German user, and the API stores `150` instead of `1.50`. Where is the bug?
choices: Locale-aware input is parsed with rules that treat the comma as a thousands separator
The database column is an integer type, which drops everything after the decimal point
The browser rounds numbers typed with a comma to the nearest whole unit before sending
JSON cannot carry decimal numbers, so the API multiplies prices by one hundred
questions.why: In German, the comma is the decimal separator; stripping 'thousands separators' before parsing turns `1,50` into `150`. Parse with the user's locale on the client (or use `<input type=number>`), and send numbers as plain JSON numbers or decimal strings.
questions.asked: Internationalisation bugs are common in CRUD forms; interviewers like 'parse at the edge, send canonical values'.

questions.q: A bug appeared some time in the last 200 commits, and you have a reliable test that shows it. What is the fastest systematic way to find the commit?
choices: Read every commit message from the last month and look for the most likely suspect
Revert the most recent commits one at a time until the test passes again
`git bisect`, which binary-searches the range and needs about eight test runs
Diff the current code against the last release and review the whole thing
questions.why: Bisect halves the range each step, so 200 commits take about log2(200) ≈ 8 checks, and `git bisect run <test>` automates it. Reverting one by one is linear and may not even revert the right thing.
questions.asked: Classic efficient-debugging question; mentioning `bisect run` with a script is a strong detail.

questions.q: A bug report says 'the export crashes for some customers'. Before changing any code, what gives you the most leverage?
choices: Rewrite the export module, since crashing code is usually poorly structured
Add retries around the export so that the crash is hidden from customers
Upgrade every dependency in case one of them has already fixed the crash
A minimal reproduction: the smallest input and steps that trigger the crash
questions.why: A reliable, small repro turns guessing into experiment: you can test hypotheses, bisect and later keep it as a regression test. Retries hide the symptom, and blanket upgrades change many variables at once.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear a method; 'first, reproduce it' is the expected opening move.

questions.q: You get this Node stack trace. Which frame should you usually read first?
questions.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')
    at formatUser (/app/src/users/format.js:12:23)
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at listUsers (/app/src/users/routes.js:40:18)
    at Layer.handle (/app/node_modules/express/lib/router/layer.js:95:5)
choices: `format.js:12`, the topmost frame in your own code where the error was thrown
`layer.js:95`, because the bottom frame is always where an error really started
`Array.map`, since built-in functions are the usual source of such errors
None of them, since stack traces in Node always point at the wrong line
questions.why: The top frame is where the exception was raised; here `formatUser` received an element that is `undefined`. Then walk down to `routes.js:40` to see why the array contained it. Framework frames at the bottom are just how the request arrived.
questions.asked: Reading a stack trace fluently is a basic skill interviewers sometimes test live.

questions.q: Staging works, production fails, and both run the same image. What is the most productive next step?
choices: Redeploy production several times, since the failure may be a one-off
Diff the two environments: config, secrets, data shape, versions and traffic
Copy the production database into staging and hope the failure reproduces
Roll back to an image from last month, even though the code is identical
questions.why: If the code is identical, the difference is in what surrounds it: environment variables, feature flags, network rules, dependency versions, data shape or volume. Listing and comparing them narrows the search; blind redeploys and rollbacks test nothing.
questions.asked: Shows a disciplined comparison method rather than trial and error.

questions.q: A new feature is behind a flag. After enabling it for 10% of users, errors rise. What should you do first?
choices: Roll the whole release back, since a flag cannot be switched off once it is enabled
Raise it to 100% so that you get enough errors to diagnose the problem well
Turn the flag off, confirm errors drop, then investigate with the flag's cohort
Leave it on and add more logging, since 10% of users is a small population
questions.why: The point of a flag is an instant kill switch: disabling it mitigates without a deploy, and checking that errors fall confirms the flag caused them. Then reproduce with the flag on in a safe environment.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know feature flags are a mitigation tool, not only a release tool.

questions.q: An API in Kubernetes keeps restarting. `kubectl describe pod` shows the liveness probe failing during start-up, which takes 40 seconds. What is the fix?
choices: Remove all probes so that Kubernetes stops restarting the container at all
Increase the pod's memory limit, since slow start-up means memory pressure
Change the restart policy to `Never` so that the pod stays up even after the failures
Add a startup probe (or initial delay) so liveness checks begin after start-up
questions.why: Liveness probes that fire before the app is ready kill it in a loop. A startup probe holds off liveness checks until the app has started; readiness then controls traffic. Removing probes loses self-healing entirely.
questions.asked: A common Kubernetes crash-loop cause; distinguishing startup, readiness and liveness probes is the key.

questions.q: A Postgres-backed endpoint was fast last month and is now slow. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows `Seq Scan on orders` with a filter on `customer_id`. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Add an index on `orders(customer_id)` so the planner can seek instead of scan
Run `VACUUM FULL` every hour so that sequential scans are turned into index scans
Increase the connection pool size, so more scans can run in parallel
Rewrite the query as a stored procedure, which always uses an index
questions.why: As the table grew, scanning every row to find one customer's orders became expensive. An index on the filter column lets Postgres jump to matching rows. Vacuuming reclaims space but does not create access paths, and more connections just run more slow scans.
questions.asked: The canonical slow-query scenario; interviewers want EXPLAIN and an index, not guesswork.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2022, a stored procedure is fast for most customers but occasionally becomes slow for everyone until the plan cache is cleared. What is the classic explanation?
choices: The procedure leaks memory, which slows every call until the server restarts
Parameter sniffing: a plan compiled for an unusual value is reused for all calls
The procedure's statistics are updated on every call, which blocks other queries
SQL Server randomly picks a plan each time, so some executions are unlucky
questions.why: The first execution's parameter values shape the cached plan; if they are atypical (a huge customer), the plan suits them and hurts everyone else. Fixes include `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`, `OPTIMIZE FOR`, or Query Store plan forcing and SQL Server 2022's parameter-sensitive plan optimisation.
questions.asked: A famous SQL Server production issue; naming it and a fix separates experienced candidates.

questions.q: After a bulk import of two million rows, queries on that Postgres table became slow, though the indexes exist. What should you try first?
choices: Drop and recreate every index on the table, since bulk imports corrupt the indexes
Restart the database server, since imports leave locks held in memory
Run `ANALYZE` so the planner's statistics reflect the new data distribution
Increase `work_mem` to the maximum so that every query has more memory
questions.why: The planner chooses plans from table statistics; after a large change they are stale until autovacuum's analyze catches up, so it may misestimate row counts and pick bad plans. Running `ANALYZE` right after bulk loads is standard.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the planner depends on statistics, not just on indexes existing.

questions.q: A SQL Server query filters `WHERE AccountCode = @code`. `AccountCode` is `varchar` with an index, but EF Core sends `@code` as `nvarchar`, and the index is scanned. Why?
choices: Indexes on `varchar` columns are ignored whenever the query uses a parameter value
EF Core disables index use for queries generated from LINQ expressions
The `nvarchar` parameter is truncated, so no index entry can match it
An implicit conversion of the column to `nvarchar` prevents an efficient seek
questions.why: SQL Server converts the lower-precedence `varchar` column to match the `nvarchar` parameter, which forces it to evaluate the conversion row by row instead of seeking. Map the property as `varchar` (`HasColumnType` or `IsUnicode(false)`) so parameters match.
questions.asked: Implicit conversions are a subtle real-world cause of scans; spotting it shows deep SQL Server experience.

questions.q: Users report that saving a record hangs for 30 seconds and then times out, but only when a nightly report is running. Where do you look first?
choices: Blocking: the report's long transaction holds locks that the update waits on
Disk space: reports write temporary files that fill the database's data disk
The CDN: reports are cached at the edge, which delays other requests
Browser limits: the report opens too many tabs for the save to go through
questions.why: A long-running reporting transaction can hold or escalate locks, so writers queue behind it until they time out. Check `pg_locks`/`pg_stat_activity` or `sys.dm_exec_requests` blocking chains; run reports on a replica or use snapshot isolation.
questions.asked: Correlating a symptom with another workload is the core skill here; strong answers name the DMVs or views.

questions.q: A Node API using `pg.Pool` with `max: 10` hangs under load, and requests never reach the database. The code below runs per request. What is the bug?
choices: `pool.connect` opens a new pool each time, which exhausts server memory
The early `return` skips `client.release()`, so clients leak until none are left
`client.query` must be called without `await` when a pool is used
`res.status(404)` closes the database connection, so the pool retries the query forever
questions.why: Every 404 path leaks a checked-out client; after ten, `pool.connect()` waits forever for one to be returned. Release in `finally`, or use `pool.query()`, which checks out and releases for you.
questions.asked: Connection leaks on early-return paths are extremely common; the try/finally fix is expected.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core API logs `Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool` under load. What does this mean?
choices: The database server is down, and the pool is reporting it with a misleading message
The connection string has an invalid timeout, so every attempt fails immediately
All pooled connections are in use (or leaked), and new requests waited too long
The pool was disposed at start-up, so no connections can ever be obtained
questions.why: ADO.NET's pool (default max 100) was exhausted: connections are held too long by slow queries, long transactions or undisposed contexts/connections. Look for missing `using`, long-running work inside a transaction, and slow queries before simply raising `Max Pool Size`.
questions.asked: A standard .NET production error; interviewers want causes, not just 'raise the pool size'.

questions.q: A Postgres server starts rejecting connections with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` after you scale the API from 4 to 20 instances. Why?
choices: Each API instance now opens a separate database, and Postgres limits databases
Postgres limits connections per client IP, and the new instances share one IP
The API instances are running an older driver that Postgres no longer supports
Each instance has its own pool, so total connections exceeded `max_connections`
questions.why: Twenty instances with a pool of 20 each want 400 connections, beyond the default 100. Size pools as `max_connections` divided by instances (with headroom), or add PgBouncer. Postgres connections are processes, so raising the limit has real memory cost.
questions.asked: Scaling out the app layer can break the database layer; interviewers like the arithmetic.

questions.q: Your logs show one request running 101 SQL queries: one for a list of orders and one per order for its customer. What is this, and what is the usual fix?
choices: N+1 queries; load the related data in one query with a join or `Include`
A deadlock; retry the request so that the queries run in a different order
Connection pooling; disable the pool so all queries share one connection
Query caching; clear the plan cache so the database batches the queries
questions.why: Lazy loading or per-item lookups turn a list into 1 + N round trips, which scales with the data. Eager loading (`Include`), a projection with a join, or batching ids into one `IN` query collapses it to one or two queries.
questions.asked: The single most-asked ORM performance question; seeing it from logs is the real-world version.

questions.q: A migration adds a column with a default value and an index to a 50-million-row Postgres table. During deploy the site stops responding for minutes. What likely happened?
choices: Adding a column with any default always rewrites every row, in all versions of Postgres
`CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` locks the table against writes until it finishes
Migrations run on every API instance at once, so the column was added 20 times
Postgres closes all connections when the schema changes, forcing reconnects
questions.why: A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes for the whole build; `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids that (outside a transaction). Since Postgres 11, adding a column with a constant default is metadata-only, so the index is the likely culprit.
questions.asked: Online schema changes separate people who have migrated big tables from those who have not.

questions.q: A user updates their profile and is redirected to the profile page, which shows the old values. A refresh a second later shows the new ones. Reads go to a replica. What is the cause?
choices: The browser cached the page, and the refresh bypassed the cache by coincidence
The write was committed twice, and the first commit was rolled back quietly
Replica lag: the redirect's read hit the replica before the write replicated
The ORM cached the entity in memory and served it from the first request
questions.why: Asynchronous replication means a replica can be milliseconds to seconds behind. Read-your-writes flows should read from the primary for a short window after a write, or return the updated data in the write response.
questions.asked: Eventual consistency made concrete; strong answers give a routing strategy.

questions.q: Two admins edit the same product. Admin A saves a new price; a minute later admin B saves a description change, and A's price is gone. What is this, and what prevents it?
choices: A deadlock; add retries so both saves eventually succeed in some order
A replication delay; always read from the primary database before showing the edit form
A cache bug; disable output caching on the edit endpoint for admins
A lost update; use optimistic concurrency with a version or rowversion check
questions.why: B's form was loaded before A saved, and saving the whole object overwrote A's change. A version column in the `WHERE` clause (EF Core concurrency tokens, `rowversion`) makes B's save fail with a conflict the UI can resolve.
questions.asked: Every CRUD app with multiple editors has this bug; the version-check answer is expected at mid-level.

questions.q: Sign-up checks `SELECT ... WHERE email = @e`, and inserts if none is found. Under load, duplicate accounts with the same email appear. What is the robust fix?
choices: A unique constraint on email, handling the violation as 'already registered'
Wrapping the check and insert in a `try/catch` block in the application code
Adding a one-second delay before the insert so the first request finishes
Checking again after the insert and deleting the second row if one exists
questions.why: Check-then-insert is a race: two requests both see 'none' and both insert. Only the database can enforce uniqueness atomically; the unique index turns the race into an error you translate to a friendly message.
questions.asked: The canonical race condition in CRUD apps; interviewers want 'let the database enforce it'.

questions.q: A payment client retries timed-out HTTP calls, and some customers are charged twice. What is the right fix?
choices: Stop retrying payment calls entirely, since any retry can double-charge
Send an idempotency key with each logical payment so the provider deduplicates
Increase the timeout to five minutes so that the first call always has time to finish
Retry only on Mondays, when the provider guarantees exactly-once delivery
questions.why: A timeout does not mean failure: the charge may have succeeded before the response was lost. An idempotency key (reused across retries of the same logical operation) lets the provider return the original result instead of charging again.
questions.asked: Payments make idempotency concrete; strong answers note that timeouts are ambiguous outcomes.

questions.q: A scheduled job runs every 5 minutes, but some runs take 8 minutes, and records are occasionally processed twice. What is the cause?
choices: The scheduler's clock drifts by three minutes, so it fires the job early
The database commits each record twice when a transaction runs for too long
Runs overlap: a new run starts before the last one finishes, and both claim records
The job's logs are duplicated, so records only appear to be processed twice
questions.why: Timer-based schedulers usually do not wait for the previous run. Prevent overlap (a lock or `DisallowConcurrentExecution`), claim work atomically (`UPDATE ... RETURNING` or `SKIP LOCKED`), and make processing idempotent.
questions.asked: Overlapping jobs are a common production bug; the strong answer covers both prevention and idempotency.

questions.q: Every authenticated request runs `UPDATE users SET last_seen = now() WHERE id = @id`. Under load, lock waits on the `users` table climb and logins slow down. What is a sensible fix?
choices: Wrap the update in a serialisable transaction so that the lock waits are shorter
Update `last_seen` only when it is older than a few minutes, or batch the writes
Move the `users` table to a separate database server so it gets more locks
Add an index on `last_seen` so the update can find the row more quickly
questions.why: A write on every request turns a read-mostly row into a hotspot that competes with logins and profile updates. Throttling the write (only if stale) or buffering it in memory or Redis and flushing in batches removes most of the contention; an extra index makes each update more expensive.
questions.asked: Shows you question whether a write is needed at all, a mark of production experience.

questions.q: Tokens issued by your auth server are rejected by one API instance with 'token not yet valid', but accepted by the others. What should you check?
choices: Clock skew: that instance's clock is behind, so the token's `nbf` looks in the future
The signing key rotated, and that instance uses a key from the future
The token is too long for that instance's header buffer, so it is truncated
That instance runs a different .NET version, which reads token dates in local time
questions.why: JWT validation compares `nbf`, `iat` and `exp` against the local clock. A server whose clock has drifted (NTP not running) rejects fresh tokens; validators allow small clock skew, but fix time sync on the host.
questions.asked: Shows you know time is a distributed-systems problem, even in a CRUD app.

questions.q: A Node 24 API becomes unresponsive for everyone whenever one user uploads a large CSV, though CPU usage is only one core at 100%. What is the likely cause?
choices: The upload saturates the network card, so other requests cannot be received
Node limits each process to one concurrent request while an upload is running
Synchronous parsing of the CSV blocks the event loop, so no other request runs
The upload uses all available memory, so the garbage collector stops the process
questions.why: Node runs JavaScript on one thread; a long synchronous loop (parsing, `JSON.parse` of huge payloads, sync crypto) stops the event loop from serving anything else. Stream the parse, chunk the work, or move it to a worker thread or background job.
questions.asked: The most important Node performance concept; interviewers expect 'blocking the event loop' and a fix.

questions.q: Which metric tells you most directly that a Node service's event loop is being blocked?
choices: Heap used, because a blocked loop always allocates more memory
Event loop delay or lag, for example from `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`
The number of open file descriptors, since blocking opens more files
Garbage collection count, since blocking the loop triggers a full collection each time
