questions.why: Event loop delay measures how late timers fire; sustained high values mean something synchronous is hogging the thread. Heap and GC metrics describe memory, which is a different problem.
questions.asked: Shows you know how to measure Node health, not just CPU and memory.

questions.q: Error rates spike for about five minutes at 00:00 UTC every night and are normal the rest of the day. What is the most productive first step?
choices: Add more instances permanently, since midnight traffic must be higher than you think
Switch the servers to local time so the spike moves out of the busiest hours
Ignore it, since a five-minute spike each night stays within most error budgets
List what is scheduled at midnight, such as cron jobs, backups and log rotation
questions.why: A spike at the same wall-clock time every day almost always correlates with scheduled work competing for the database, locks or CPU, or with daily expiries. Line up job schedules against the graphs before changing capacity.
questions.asked: Correlation with time is a basic but powerful debugging move; interviewers like the list of usual suspects.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core endpoint serves videos with `return File(await System.IO.File.ReadAllBytesAsync(path), "video/mp4");`. With a few concurrent 2 GB downloads, the process runs out of memory. What is the fix?
choices: Increase the container memory to 16 GB so that several videos fit at once
Compress each video with gzip before returning it, so the arrays are smaller
Return a stream (`PhysicalFile` or a `FileStream`) so the file is sent in chunks
Call `GC.Collect()` after each download so the byte arrays are freed sooner
questions.why: `ReadAllBytesAsync` loads the entire file into one huge array per request (on the large object heap). Returning `PhysicalFile(path, ...)` or a `FileStream` streams from disk with small buffers and supports range requests; video is already compressed, and forcing GCs does not reduce peak use.
questions.asked: Buffering versus streaming is a basic but frequently missed concept in file endpoints.

questions.q: A .NET 9 API allocates a fresh 200 KB `byte[]` buffer per request, and `dotnet-counters` shows frequent gen 2 collections with long pauses. Why?
choices: Arrays over 85,000 bytes go on the large object heap, which is only collected in gen 2
Byte arrays are pinned by the runtime, so every single collection has to scan them twice
The GC promotes any object that survives one request straight to gen 2 storage
Server GC collects only gen 2, so every allocation eventually causes a full GC
questions.why: Large objects skip the cheap gen 0 path and are reclaimed only by full, expensive gen 2 collections, so churning big buffers triggers them often. Rent buffers from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` or stream instead of buffering.
questions.asked: The LOH is a classic .NET performance topic; `ArrayPool` is the answer that shows you have fixed it.

questions.q: A Node API gets steadily slower over each week, and speed returns after every deploy. CPU per request rises; memory is flat. What pattern fits best?
choices: A memory leak, since slower responses always mean the heap is growing
An in-memory list that grows over time and is scanned on each request
The database needs a restart each week, which the deploy does as well
The CDN's cache warms up after deploys and slowly empties over the week
questions.why: Rising CPU per request with flat memory suggests work proportional to accumulated state, such as an array of revoked tokens or registered handlers scanned linearly on every call; the restart resets it. Profile a slow request and look for a loop over something that only grows.
questions.asked: Tests reasoning from symptoms (resets on restart, CPU not memory) to a class of bug.

questions.q: A React SPA gets slower the longer a tab stays open, and DevTools shows detached DOM nodes growing. What is a common cause?
choices: React 19 keeps every previous render in memory so that it can undo changes
An effect subscribes to a global event or timer and never cleans it up
CSS animations keep the DOM nodes they animated alive for the session
The browser caches each API response as DOM nodes until the tab closes
questions.why: A listener on `window`, a `setInterval` or a third-party subscription created in an effect without a cleanup function keeps closures, and through them old components and DOM nodes, reachable after unmount. Return a cleanup from the effect.
questions.asked: Frontend leaks are underrated; the cleanup-function answer ties to how effects are meant to work.

questions.q: A .NET 9 API's working set grows under load and never shrinks back, but it does not crash, and a memory dump shows nothing unusual. What is a reasonable explanation?
choices: Every .NET app leaks memory by design, which is why IIS recycles app pools
The garbage collector is broken in .NET 9 and must be switched off in config
The GC keeps memory it has committed for reuse, so a plateau is normal
The app is out of disk space, so the operating system cannot page it out
questions.why: Server GC is tuned for throughput and holds on to committed memory to avoid re-requesting it; a high but stable plateau is not a leak. A leak keeps growing across GCs. In containers, set limits and consider `DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit` or DATAS in .NET 9.
questions.asked: Separates 'uses memory' from 'leaks memory', which many candidates conflate.

questions.q: Which tool would you use first to watch GC counts, thread pool queue length and exception rate of a running .NET process without restarting it?
choices: `dotnet build --verbose`, which prints runtime metrics during compilation
`dotnet test`, which runs the process under a profiler and reports metrics
Visual Studio's Immediate window, attached to the production process
`dotnet-counters monitor`, which reads the runtime's live event counters
questions.why: `dotnet-counters` attaches to a running process and shows live runtime metrics (GC, thread pool, exceptions, ASP.NET Core requests). For deeper work, `dotnet-trace` captures CPU traces and `dotnet-dump` captures memory.
questions.asked: Knowing the diagnostics tools by name shows you have debugged .NET beyond breakpoints.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core API handles a burst badly: CPU is low, yet requests queue for seconds, and `dotnet-counters` shows the thread pool queue growing. The code calls `.Result` on async HTTP calls. What is happening?
choices: Thread pool starvation: blocking on async work ties up threads faster than new ones arrive
The HTTP client has a default limit of two connections per server, so calls queue
Kestrel's request queue is full, so it must be enlarged in configuration
The garbage collector pauses every thread while `.Result` values are stored
questions.why: Sync-over-async blocks pool threads waiting for work that needs pool threads to complete; the pool grows slowly, so latency spikes while CPU idles. Make the call chain async all the way down.
questions.asked: Thread pool starvation is the classic .NET production performance bug; low CPU with high latency is the tell.

questions.q: Password-reset emails worked in testing, but in production most users never receive them, and the email provider's dashboard shows them as delivered. Where do you look?
choices: The reset tokens, since expired tokens stop the email from being delivered
The users' passwords, since the provider drops mail to accounts that are locked
The app's SMTP timeout, since slow sends are silently cancelled by the provider
Spam filtering: check SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the sending domain and the headers
questions.why: 'Delivered' means the receiving server accepted it, not that it reached the inbox. Without SPF and DKIM records authorising your provider (and a DMARC policy), mail from a new domain is often junked. Check the raw headers of a test message for authentication results.
questions.asked: A common launch-week bug; strong answers know 'delivered' is not 'in the inbox'.

questions.q: A profile shows your API spends most CPU time in one function. In a flame graph, what does a very WIDE bar mean?
choices: The function was called by the most distinct callers in the code base
The function has the deepest call stack below it in the whole trace
The function, including what it calls, was on the stack for many samples
The function was the most recently executed code at the moment the trace was stopped
questions.why: Width is the proportion of samples in which that frame (and its children) was on the stack, so wide means expensive; height is just stack depth. Look for wide plateaus near the top, where time is spent in the function itself.
questions.asked: Reading a flame graph is a practical skill; interviewers sometimes show one and ask where to look.

questions.q: After an upgrade, p50 latency is unchanged but p99 doubled. What does that tell you?
choices: Nothing, because p99 is too noisy to be meaningful for real users
Every request got slower, but the median hides it because of rounding
The slowdown must be in the database, since the API code itself is unchanged by the upgrade
A minority of requests got much slower, such as some paths, users or GC pauses
questions.why: Percentiles describe the distribution: the typical request is the same, but the slowest 1% got worse. Slice by endpoint, tenant and instance, and check GC or lock waits; averages would hide this entirely.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand percentiles, a basic observability literacy check.

questions.q: Your tracing samples 1% of requests. A customer reports one very slow checkout, but you cannot find its trace. What sampling approach would have kept it?
choices: Tail-based sampling, which decides after the request whether it was slow or failed
Head-based sampling at 0.1%, which keeps fewer but more representative traces overall
Turning tracing off and relying on logs, which always record every request
Sampling by user id, which guarantees every customer's first request is kept
questions.why: Head sampling decides at the start, before anyone knows the request will be slow, so rare bad requests are usually dropped. Tail sampling (in an OpenTelemetry Collector) keeps errors and slow traces plus a sample of the rest.
questions.asked: Shows understanding of the trade-offs in tracing cost and usefulness.

questions.q: An order request enqueues a message, and a worker processes it later. In the logs you cannot connect the worker's error to the original request. What is missing?
choices: A shared log file that both the API and the worker write to on disk
Passing the trace or correlation id in the message and logging it in the worker
Synchronous processing, since queues make request tracing impossible
A higher log level on the worker so that it records every message body
questions.why: Context does not cross a queue automatically: put the trace or correlation id in the message headers and restore it in the consumer (OpenTelemetry does this with links or propagation). Logging whole payloads adds volume, not linkage.
questions.asked: Asynchronous boundaries are where tracing breaks; the strong answer propagates context explicitly.

questions.q: Logs show `Error: Something went wrong` with no stack trace or context, thrown from deep in your Node app. What change most improves future debugging?
choices: Log the error at `debug` level so it only appears when needed
Catch errors at every function and return `null`, so nothing crashes
Throw errors with a specific message and a `cause`, and log them with context
Replace errors with `console.log` calls so the output is always visible
questions.why: A descriptive message, the original error attached via `new Error('...', { cause })`, and structured logging of the stack plus request id make an error traceable. Swallowing errors and returning `null` moves the crash somewhere even harder to diagnose.
questions.asked: Error hygiene is a practical signal of seniority; `cause` shows you know modern JavaScript.

questions.q: A Node process crashes and restarts several times a day with no error in the logs. What is a likely gap?
choices: Node never logs errors in production mode, so crashes are always silent
The restarts are caused by log rotation, which kills processes by design
Unhandled promise rejections are ignored by Node 24, so they cannot crash the process
No `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` logging, or the platform's OOM kill
questions.why: Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process, and if nothing logs it before exit, you see only restarts. Also check container events for OOMKilled, which leaves no application log at all.
questions.asked: Silent crash loops happen; the strong answer checks both the app's last words and the platform's events.

questions.q: Your API runs on six instances, and the error rate has risen, but only instance 4 is producing the errors. What is the best first move?
choices: Roll back the latest release on all six instances before looking any further
Take instance 4 out of rotation or replace it, then compare it with a healthy one
Scale out to twelve instances so that instance 4 receives a smaller share of traffic
Restart the database, since one instance erroring points to a data problem
questions.why: Errors isolated to one instance point at something local to it: a bad host, full disk, stale config or a failed start-up step. Draining it mitigates immediately, and diffing it against a healthy peer finds the cause; a code bug would hit every instance.
questions.asked: Tests whether you slice metrics by instance before acting; strong answers mitigate first, then compare.

questions.q: When is 'fix forward' preferable to rolling back a bad release?
choices: Always, since rollbacks are riskier than any fix you can write under pressure
When the release ran an irreversible change, such as a destructive migration
Never, because good teams must always be able to roll back every change
Only when the release happened more than a week ago and nobody remembers it
questions.why: If the old code cannot run against the new schema or data, rolling back makes things worse, so a small, reviewed forward fix is the path. That is why migrations are designed to be backward-compatible (expand, migrate, contract).
questions.asked: Shows judgement rather than dogma; strong answers connect it to backward-compatible migrations.

questions.q: During an incident, several engineers are changing configuration and restarting services at the same time. What does a good incident process add first?
choices: A rule that only the most senior engineer may touch production systems
A ban on communicating until the root cause has been found, agreed and written up
A single incident lead who coordinates actions, plus a running log of changes
A requirement to open a pull request for every command during the outage
questions.why: Uncoordinated changes confuse cause and effect and can make things worse. An incident commander assigns work, approves changes, and someone records a timeline, which also feeds the postmortem.
questions.asked: Tests awareness of incident roles; a timeline and a single lead are the key points.

questions.q: An alert fires at 3 a.m. for a service the on-call engineer has never worked on. What most reduces the time to mitigate?
choices: A rule that only the service's original author may respond to its alerts
A dashboard with every metric the service emits, in no particular order
A runbook linked from the alert, with checks and safe mitigation steps
A longer alert delay, so that the owning team sees it in the morning
questions.why: A runbook turns tribal knowledge into steps: what the alert means, which dashboards to check, and safe actions such as rollback, scale or flag off. Unstructured dashboards leave a stranger guessing, and waiting until morning extends user impact.
questions.asked: Operational maturity question; strong answers say every paging alert should link to one.

questions.q: During a 40-minute outage, customers and support staff keep asking what is happening. The cause is still unknown. What should the team communicate?
choices: Nothing until the root cause is known, to avoid saying anything that turns out wrong
A detailed technical explanation of every hypothesis the team is investigating
A promise that the outage will be fixed within five minutes, to calm customers
Regular updates on impact and status, with the time of the next update
questions.why: People mostly need to know you are aware, what is affected and when they will hear more; a status page and a named communicator keep engineers free to work. Silence breeds escalations, and guesses or promises create a second credibility problem.
questions.asked: Incident communication is part of the job; interviewers like 'next update at' as a habit.

questions.q: A queue consumer reports 'processed' for each message, but downstream data is often missing. The handler below is used. What is the bug?
choices: `JSON.parse` is synchronous, so it must be awaited before the message can be saved
The message is acknowledged before the save, so a failed save loses it for good
`async` handlers cannot be used with queues, so every message is dropped
`msg.ack()` should be called twice, once before and once after the save
questions.why: Acknowledging first removes the message from the queue, so if `saveToDb` throws or the process dies, nothing redelivers it. Acknowledge after the work succeeds, and make the handler idempotent to cope with redelivery.
questions.asked: Acknowledgement order is basic but frequently wrong in real code.

questions.q: A consumer's messages reappear and are processed a second time even though processing succeeds. Each message takes about 90 seconds; the visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Why?
choices: The broker duplicates every message by default to guarantee delivery
The acknowledgement is too large to be accepted after 30 seconds
The timeout expires mid-processing, so the broker redelivers it to another consumer
Processing succeeds only on the second attempt, since the first is a warm-up
questions.why: If a message is not acknowledged within its visibility timeout or lock duration, the broker assumes the consumer died and redelivers it. Set the timeout above the worst-case processing time or extend the lock while working.
questions.asked: A common queue misconfiguration; strong answers mention lock renewal as well as a longer timeout.

questions.q: A consumer group's lag keeps growing during peak hours and recovers overnight. What does that tell you?
choices: Messages are being lost at peak times, and lag measures how many were lost
The broker is slowing down deliberately to protect itself from overload
The producers are sending duplicates, so lag always doubles during peaks
Consumers process more slowly than producers publish during peaks
questions.why: Lag is the backlog between the newest message and what consumers have processed. Growing lag means consumption rate is below production rate; scale consumers on lag, speed up handlers, or accept delay if the business can.
questions.asked: Basic queue operations literacy; autoscaling on lag is the strong follow-up.

questions.q: A downstream API was down for a minute. When it recovered, every client retried at the same instant and knocked it over again. What should the clients do?
choices: Retry with exponential backoff and random jitter, capped at a few attempts
Retry immediately in a tight loop so that they succeed first when it recovers
Never retry at all, since retries are what caused the second outage
Retry exactly every five seconds, so the load is spread evenly in time
questions.why: Fixed or immediate retries synchronise clients into a thundering herd. Exponential backoff reduces the rate and jitter de-synchronises them; a circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly down.
questions.asked: Retry design comes up in every resilience discussion; 'jitter' is the word interviewers wait for.

questions.q: After adding a Redis cache to `GET /api/dashboard`, a user reports seeing another customer's figures. What is the most likely bug?
choices: Redis replicated the key to a replica that belongs to the other customer
The cache TTL is too long, so figures from last week are being shown
The cache key omits the user or tenant id, so everyone shares one entry
Redis compresses values, which mixes up entries that are the same size
questions.why: If the key is just the route, the first caller's personalised response is served to everyone. Include every input that changes the response (tenant, user, role, query) in the key, or cache only data that is genuinely shared.
questions.asked: A real data-leak pattern; strong answers treat cache keys as part of the security model.

questions.q: After editing a product, admins see the change, but customers see the old price for up to ten minutes. Product data is cached in Redis with a 10-minute TTL. What is the fix?
choices: Lower the TTL to one second so that the cache is effectively switched off
Cache product data in each browser instead, so the server cache is not used
Invalidate or update the product's cache entry as part of the write
Add a second Redis instance so that reads are split between two caches
questions.why: Time-based expiry alone guarantees staleness up to the TTL. Deleting (or rewriting) the key when the product changes gives immediate consistency for the common path, with the TTL as a safety net.
questions.asked: Invalidation is the hard part of caching; interviewers want invalidate-on-write.

questions.q: A background worker crashes on start-up with `Cannot access a disposed context instance` after resolving a `DbContext` in its constructor. The worker is an `IHostedService` (a singleton). What is wrong?
choices: `DbContext` cannot be used in background services under any circumstances
The database connection string is missing from the worker's configuration
EF Core 9 disposes every context after five minutes of inactivity by default in workers
A scoped `DbContext` is captured by a singleton; create a scope per unit of work
questions.why: Hosted services live for the whole app, but `DbContext` is scoped. Inject `IServiceScopeFactory`, create a scope for each job or message, and resolve the context from it, so each unit of work gets a fresh context.
questions.asked: The captive-dependency bug in its most common real form; the scope-factory fix is expected.

questions.q: An EF Core 9 request throws `A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed`. What is the usual cause?
choices: Running two queries on the same context concurrently, e.g. with `Task.WhenAll`
Calling `SaveChangesAsync` twice in a row within the same request's unit of work
Using `AsNoTracking`, which makes the context refuse a second query
Having two `DbSet` properties that point at the same database table
questions.why: `DbContext` is not thread-safe and supports one operation at a time; awaiting several queries in parallel on it triggers this. Await them sequentially, or use separate contexts (for example via `IDbContextFactory`) for true parallelism.
questions.asked: A common EF Core mistake when people first try to 'speed up' a request with parallel queries.

questions.q: A SQL Server app sees deadlocks between two transactions that update `Orders` and `Customers`. What is a common structural fix?
choices: Wrap every statement in `NOLOCK` hints so that no locks are ever taken
Make every transaction touch shared tables in the same order
Raise the lock timeout so that deadlocked transactions wait longer
Move the two tables into separate databases so they cannot deadlock
questions.why: Deadlocks need a cycle: A holds Orders and wants Customers while B holds Customers and wants Orders. A consistent access order removes the cycle; short transactions and retrying the victim handle the rest. `NOLOCK` only affects reads and brings dirty reads.
questions.asked: Goes beyond 'retry the victim'; consistent lock ordering is the structural answer.

questions.q: A Postgres database's disk usage keeps growing though row counts are flat, and queries on a busy `sessions` table are slowing. What should you check?
choices: Whether the table has too many columns, which Postgres stores twice on disk for safety
Whether the server's clock is wrong, which stops rows being counted
Bloat from dead tuples, and whether autovacuum keeps up with the updates
Whether indexes were created in a different tablespace from the table
questions.why: Postgres updates and deletes leave dead row versions (MVCC) that vacuum must reclaim. On high-churn tables, autovacuum can fall behind, or a long-open transaction can stop it; tune per-table autovacuum settings and find idle-in-transaction sessions.
questions.asked: MVCC and vacuum are Postgres-specific depth that interviewers at Postgres shops probe.

questions.q: A query takes 20 ms when you run it by hand in `psql`, but 4 seconds when the app runs it through EF Core. What should you do first?
choices: Rewrite the query as raw SQL, since EF Core always generates slower queries
Capture the exact SQL and parameter values the app sends, then EXPLAIN that
Add `AsNoTracking()`, since change tracking accounts for most query time
Assume the network is slow and move the database next to the app server
questions.why: The app often runs something different: other joins from `Include`, a parameterised statement that gets a generic plan, or different parameter types. Log the generated SQL (`LogTo`, `ToQueryString()`), run EXPLAIN ANALYZE with the real parameters, and compare plans.
questions.asked: Tests whether you compare like with like before blaming the ORM.

questions.q: A developer restored last night's production database into staging to reproduce a bug. An hour later, real customers complain about receiving strange test emails. What was missing?
choices: A faster restore, so that the test could finish before the email job started up
Scrubbing personal data and pointing staging's email at a sandbox or catch-all
A read replica, so that staging could read production data without copying it
A different staging database password, so the email job could not connect
questions.why: Production data carries real addresses, and staging jobs happily act on them. Anonymise copies before use and configure non-production environments to send mail only to a sandbox such as Mailpit or the provider's test mode.
questions.asked: A surprisingly common incident; strong answers mention both data masking and sandboxed integrations.

questions.q: Users report being logged out almost exactly one hour after signing in, even while actively using the app. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The browser clears all cookies once an hour for privacy reasons
The server restarts every hour, which invalidates every session held in its memory
The access token expires after an hour and the refresh flow is not working
The load balancer moves each user to a new instance once per hour
questions.why: A precise, repeatable interval points at a configured lifetime. Access tokens are short-lived by design; the client should use the refresh token before or on a 401. Check the refresh request in the network tab and the token lifetimes in the identity provider.
questions.asked: Tests reasoning from 'exactly one hour' to a configured expiry rather than guessing.

questions.q: A download link built as `'/files/' + name` works for most files, but `Q3 report #2.pdf` returns 404. Why?
choices: Unencoded characters such as `#` change the URL, so encode it with `encodeURIComponent`
Browsers refuse to download files whose names contain digits and spaces
The server's filesystem cannot store names containing `#`, so the file was never saved
PDF files must be served from a separate domain when their names have symbols
questions.why: `#` starts the fragment, which is never sent to the server, and spaces, `?` and `%` also have meaning in URLs. Encode each path segment with `encodeURIComponent`, or better, link by a stored id rather than the user's filename.
questions.asked: URL encoding bugs are everyday work; strong answers suggest using ids instead of user-supplied names.

questions.q: Searching customers works, except a search for `O'Brien` returns HTTP 500. What does that most strongly suggest?
choices: The database cannot store apostrophes, so the customer was saved incorrectly
The search index has not been rebuilt since the customer was created
The apostrophe exceeds the maximum length allowed for a search term
The SQL is built by string concatenation, which is also an injection hole
questions.why: The quote closes the SQL string literal, producing a syntax error, which means user input reaches the SQL text directly. Use parameterised queries; escaping by hand is fragile. This bug is the friendly version of SQL injection.
questions.asked: Connects a mundane bug to a security flaw, which is exactly what interviewers want to hear.

questions.q: You renamed the JSON field `fullName` to `displayName` in the API. The web app was updated in the same deploy, but older mobile app versions now show blank names. What should you have done?
choices: Released the mobile app first, since the stores publish every update within the hour
Added `displayName` alongside `fullName` and removed the old field only later
Returned HTTP 410 for old clients so that they are forced to upgrade
Renamed the field in the database as well, so the API stays consistent
questions.why: Clients you do not deploy (mobile apps, partners, cached SPAs) keep using the old contract. Make additive changes, keep the old field until usage drops, or version the API; removals are breaking changes.
questions.asked: API evolution question in scenario form; strong answers say 'add, then deprecate, then remove'.

questions.q: A fix was merged to `main` last week, but the bug still happens in production. How do you quickly check whether the deployed release includes the fix?
choices: Read the release notes, which list every commit that each release contains
Search the production logs for the fix's commit message text
Run `git tag --contains <fix-sha>` and compare with the deployed version
Ask the team whether anyone remembers deploying since the merge
questions.why: `git tag --contains` (or `git branch -r --contains`) lists the tags or branches that include a commit; compare that with the version the app reports. Release notes and memory are often incomplete, and commit messages are not logged at runtime.
questions.asked: Shows fluency with git as a debugging tool, and the habit of verifying before assuming.

questions.q: Password-reset emails in production contain links to `http://localhost:5173/reset?...`. What is the fix?
choices: Read the public base URL from per-environment config instead of hard-coding it
Build the link from the request's `Origin` header, which browsers always send with it
Ask users to replace `localhost` with the real domain before clicking
Send the reset token in the email body so that no link is needed at all
questions.why: Links in emails must use the public site URL, which differs per environment, so it belongs in configuration validated at start-up. Deriving it from untrusted headers risks host-header poisoning of reset links.
questions.asked: A classic 'worked in dev' bug; mentioning host-header poisoning is a strong security detail.

questions.q: A nightly sync calls a partner API 5,000 times in a tight loop and starts getting HTTP 429 after the first few hundred. What should the client do?
choices: Retry each 429 immediately, since rate limits reset every second
Run the loop from several servers at once so that each one stays under the rate limit
Ignore the 429s, since the partner will process the requests later
Throttle requests and honour the `Retry-After` header when it is sent
questions.why: 429 means you exceeded the partner's rate limit; `Retry-After` says when to try again. Pacing requests (a concurrency limit or token bucket) avoids hitting it; spreading across servers to evade limits usually breaches the terms and gets keys revoked.
questions.asked: Being a good API citizen is expected; strong answers mention batching endpoints if the partner offers them.

questions.q: The frontend receives the string `"{\"id\":1}"` instead of an object, so `data.id` is undefined. The API handler does `res.json(JSON.stringify(order))`. What is wrong?
choices: `res.json` expects a Buffer, so the string should be converted first
The object is serialised twice: once by `JSON.stringify` and again by `res.json`
The frontend needs `await res.text()` instead, since JSON cannot hold nested objects
`JSON.stringify` escapes quotes only in Node, so browsers misread the result
questions.why: `res.json` already serialises its argument, so passing a string produces a JSON string literal containing JSON. Pass the object itself. The same happens in .NET when returning a pre-serialised string from `Ok(...)`.
questions.asked: A common beginner bug that looks mysterious in the network tab; recognising it is quick credit.

questions.q: The frontend logs `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<', "<!doctype "... is not valid JSON` when calling `/api/orders`. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The API returned JSON with a byte-order mark that the parser cannot read
The browser's JSON parser does not support arrays at the top level
The request received an HTML page, such as an error page or SPA fallback
The API's JSON contains a `<` character inside one of the string values
questions.why: The body starts with `<`, so it is HTML: a proxy error page, a login redirect, or the dev server returning `index.html` because the API route or proxy is wrong. Check the response in the network tab and the request URL.
questions.asked: One of the most common frontend errors; the network tab is the expected first stop.

questions.q: In VS Code, breakpoints in your TypeScript files are never hit when you debug the Node API, though the code runs. What is the usual cause?
choices: Node ignores breakpoints unless the code is run with administrator rights
Breakpoints only work in the browser, never in server-side TypeScript
The debugger needs the `--inspect-brk` flag removed from the start command to attach
The debugger runs compiled JavaScript without source maps linking it to the `.ts`
questions.why: The debugger sets breakpoints in the JavaScript that actually runs; without `sourceMap: true` (and the launch config's `outFiles` or a loader that emits maps), it cannot map your `.ts` lines to it. Enable source maps or run TypeScript via a loader that provides them.
questions.asked: Practical tooling question; being able to use a debugger properly is a mid-level expectation.

questions.q: After each deploy of a .NET API, the first few requests take several seconds, then everything is fast. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Warm-up: JIT, connection pools, caches and the DI graph are built on first use
The load balancer sends the first requests to the old version before switching over
The database locks every table for a few seconds whenever a new app version starts
The CDN rejects requests until it has downloaded the new version from the origin
questions.why: A fresh process compiles code paths, opens database connections and fills caches on the first requests. Warm-up requests before marking the instance ready, readiness probes, and ReadyToRun or Native AOT reduce the effect.
questions.asked: Shows you understand runtime start-up costs and how to keep users from paying them.

questions.q: A user reports that clicking Save does nothing. There is no error on screen. What should you check first?
choices: The server logs for that user, since the problem must be on the backend
The database, since the save may have been blocked by a lock
The source code of the Save button, reading it line by line from the top to the bottom
The browser console and network tab, to see whether a request was sent at all
questions.why: The first split is client versus server: an exception in the click handler means no request is ever sent, while a failed request shows its status and body. That one observation halves the search space.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have a systematic first step, which is what interviewers want in debugging questions.

questions.q: A bug reproduces in your normal browser window but not in a private window. What does that suggest?
choices: The bug is on the server, since private windows are routed to a different set of servers
State stored in the browser, such as cookies, localStorage, cache or extensions
Private windows run an older JavaScript engine that hides the bug
The bug depends on screen size, since private windows open smaller
questions.why: A private window starts with no cookies, storage or cached files and usually no extensions. If the bug vanishes there, inspect stored state (an old token, a stale cached bundle, a corrupt localStorage value) or disable extensions one by one.
questions.asked: A quick, cheap experiment that narrows things fast; interviewers like hearing it.

questions.q: Every page errors for one specific customer, and works for everyone else, including staff impersonating other accounts. What is the most productive next step?
choices: Look at that customer's data for an unusual value, such as a null or huge list
Ask the customer to reinstall their browser and clear every cookie it has stored for you
Roll back the latest deploy, since one customer failing means a code bug
Scale out the API, since that customer's requests may be timing out
questions.why: If the code path is shared and only one account breaks, the difference is almost always data: a missing relation, an unexpected null, an enormous collection or an odd character. Reproduce by impersonating that account in a safe environment.
questions.asked: Shows you think 'what is different about this case' before touching code.

questions.q: Support says production still behaves like the old version after a deploy. What is the most reliable way to confirm which version is actually running?
choices: Check the date on the latest commit in the repository's main branch
Compare the page's look with screenshots taken before the deploy
Ask the CI system whether the deploy pipeline finished with a green status for the release
Expose the build's commit SHA or version via a `/version` endpoint or header
questions.why: A green pipeline does not prove which bits serve traffic: a deploy can target the wrong slot, a CDN can serve old assets, or one instance can lag. Having every build report its own SHA settles it in seconds.
questions.asked: A cheap practice that saves hours; interviewers like candidates who build observability into releases.

questions.q: The React form accepts a phone number, but the API rejects it with 400. Validation rules were written separately for client and server. What is the durable fix?
choices: Remove the server-side validation, since the client already checks the input
Keep the server authoritative and share or derive the rules from one schema
Remove the client-side validation, since duplicate rules always drift apart
Ask users to type phone numbers without spaces, as stated in the placeholder
questions.why: Server validation is mandatory, since clients can be bypassed; client validation is for fast feedback. Sharing one schema (for example Zod shared in a TypeScript monorepo, or generating client rules from the API's OpenAPI description) stops them drifting, and the UI should display the server's field errors.
questions.asked: Validation duplication is a real maintenance problem; strong answers keep the server authoritative.

questions.q: In the browser, `fetch('/api/orders')` rejects with `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, and there is no HTTP status. What does that tell you?
choices: The server returned a 500 error, which fetch reports as a rejection without a status code
The JSON in the response was invalid, so fetch could not read the body
No usable HTTP response reached the page: a network, DNS, TLS or CORS failure
The request succeeded, but the page navigated away before it could be read
questions.why: `fetch` only rejects when it cannot get a response it is allowed to expose; any HTTP status, even 500, resolves normally. The console and network tab show which: a CORS block, a refused connection, a certificate error or being offline.
questions.asked: Separates transport failures from HTTP errors, a distinction many juniors miss.

questions.q: For some users one widget never appears, and the network tab shows `net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT` for `/api/ads-summary`. What is happening?
choices: The server blocked those users' IP addresses after too many requests
The CDN rejected the request because its cache key was too long
The browser's CORS policy blocked the request because of its path
A browser extension such as an ad blocker blocked the URL by pattern
questions.why: `ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT` means something in the browser, almost always a content blocker, cancelled the request; URLs containing words like `ads`, `track` or `analytics` are common targets. Rename the endpoint and do not let core features depend on such paths.
questions.asked: A real-world gotcha that is quick to diagnose if you know the error string.

questions.q: The frontend build in CI fails with `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory`. What is a reasonable first fix?
choices: Raise the build's heap with `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096`
Delete the lockfile so that npm installs smaller versions of each package
Switch the CI runner's operating system, since Linux limits Node memory
Split the build across two CI jobs that each compile half of the files
questions.why: Large bundles and type checks can exceed V8's default heap, and the flag raises the limit for that process (within the runner's RAM). If it keeps growing, look for heavy source maps, huge JSON imports or a leaking plugin.
questions.asked: A common CI failure; knowing `NODE_OPTIONS` shows hands-on build experience.

questions.q: Two services log in local time on servers in different time zones, and an incident timeline built from their logs looks out of order. What prevents this?
choices: Log timestamps in UTC using ISO 8601 with an offset, everywhere
Log the server's name alongside each message so readers can adjust
Sort all log lines alphabetically before building a timeline from them
Log only the time of day, since the date is the same for both services
questions.why: UTC timestamps with explicit offsets sort correctly and compare across machines and daylight-saving changes. Log platforms then display them in the reader's zone. Trace ids help correlate, but timestamps still need a common reference.
questions.asked: Basic logging hygiene; strong answers mention both UTC and structured timestamps.

questions.q: After `git pull`, the Node app crashes on start with `Cannot find module 'zod'`. It worked before the pull. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Reinstall Node, since pulling new code sometimes corrupts the runtime
Add `zod` to `.gitignore`, since it should not be tracked by git
Run `npm install` (or `npm ci`), because someone added a dependency
Delete `package.json`, since it is out of date after the pull
questions.why: `node_modules` is not in git; when a teammate adds a dependency to `package.json` and the lockfile, you must install to get it. Tools such as a `postmerge` hook or `npm ci` in scripts make this automatic.
questions.asked: A basic but real everyday issue; interviewers use it to check you understand what git tracks.

questions.q: Since last night every call to a partner's API fails with a TLS error, while your own site and other integrations are fine. Nothing was deployed. What should you check?
choices: Your own certificate, since outbound calls present it to the partner
The partner's certificate, which may have expired or changed its chain
Your database, since TLS failures usually mean the connection pool is full
Your firewall, since TLS errors mean port 443 has been blocked outbound
questions.why: Outbound HTTPS verifies the partner's certificate, so an expired or misconfigured one on their side breaks you with no change on yours. Check it with `openssl s_client` or a browser, and tell the partner; never disable validation as a fix.
questions.asked: Tests knowing which side's certificate matters, and resisting the 'turn off validation' shortcut.

questions.q: The `status` column stores a C# enum as an integer. After someone inserted a new member at the top of the enum, existing orders show the wrong status. Why?
choices: EF Core re-reads enum values alphabetically each time the app starts up
The database converts integers to strings whenever the enum definition in code changes
Adding an enum member invalidates the EF Core model, so all reads return 0
Enum members get sequential values by default, so every later value shifted
questions.why: Without explicit values, C# numbers members from 0 in declaration order, so inserting one renumbers the rest while the stored integers stay put. Assign explicit values, append new members, or store enums as strings.
questions.asked: A quiet data-corruption bug; interviewers like explicit values or string storage in the answer.

questions.q: Production .NET exception logs show stack traces without file names or line numbers, which makes them hard to use. What is missing?
choices: Debug builds, since Release builds cannot record exceptions at all
A try/catch in every single method, so that each frame can log its own line number
Symbol files (PDBs, portable or embedded) deployed alongside the assemblies
Verbose logging, since line numbers are only printed at `Trace` level
questions.why: Line information comes from PDBs; if the publish step strips them, traces show only method names. Embed portable PDBs (`DebugType` embedded) or ship them with the build; Release builds still produce useful traces.
questions.asked: A practical detail that makes production debugging much faster.

questions.q: Photos uploaded from phones sometimes appear sideways in your app, though they look correct in the phone's gallery. What is the cause?
choices: The camera saved the pixels unrotated with an EXIF orientation flag you ignore
The upload was corrupted in transit, which rotated part of the image data by 90 degrees
Browsers rotate portrait images by 90 degrees unless their CSS forbids it
Object storage rotates images to landscape to save space in its index
questions.why: Phones often store sensor-oriented pixels plus an orientation tag; galleries honour the tag, while server-side resizing that strips metadata loses it. Apply the orientation during processing (for example `sharp().rotate()`), then strip EXIF, which also removes location data.
questions.asked: A real upload bug; strong answers also mention stripping location metadata for privacy.

questions.q: A CSV import reads the header row, but `row.id` is always undefined even though the first column is clearly `id`. The file came from Excel. What is going on?
choices: Excel saves every header in uppercase, so the column is really called `ID` in the file
The file starts with a UTF-8 byte-order mark, which is glued to the first header
CSV parsers skip the first column unless it contains numbers
Excel adds a trailing space to every header, so the key is `id `
questions.why: Excel's 'CSV UTF-8' export begins with a BOM (U+FEFF), which is invisible in most editors but becomes part of the first field. Strip it before parsing, or use a parser option such as `bom: true`.
questions.asked: An invisible-character bug that takes hours if you do not know it; the length check is the giveaway.

questions.q: Users with emails like `bob+shop@x.com` get 'user not found' on a lookup that passes the email in the query string. What is happening?
choices: Email addresses containing `+` are invalid by the RFC, so the lookup fails correctly
The server lowercases emails, and `+` has no lowercase form to match
The browser strips `+` from every URL before sending it to the server
In query strings `+` decodes as a space, so the value must be percent-encoded
questions.why: Form-style query decoding turns `+` into a space. Build URLs with `URLSearchParams` or `encodeURIComponent`, which encode `+` as `%2B`, instead of concatenating raw values.
questions.asked: Plus-addressing is common; interviewers like candidates who build URLs with proper encoders.

questions.q: In SQL Server, customer names such as `李明` are saved as `??`. The app sends them correctly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The column is `varchar` with a non-UTF-8 collation, so unmappable characters become `?`
SQL Server cannot store characters outside the Latin alphabet in any column type
The JSON serialiser in .NET replaces non-ASCII characters with question marks
The connection string is missing `Encrypt=true`, which garbles non-ASCII text
questions.why: `varchar` uses the collation's code page; characters it cannot represent are replaced with `?` and the original is lost. Use `nvarchar`, or a `_UTF8` collation (SQL Server 2019+), for text that may contain any language.
questions.asked: Unicode storage is a classic data-loss bug; knowing `nvarchar` versus `varchar` is expected in .NET shops.

questions.q: After the database password was rotated, every API request returns 500, yet the load balancer reports all instances healthy. What does that reveal?
choices: The load balancer caches health results for a whole day, so it has not noticed yet
The health endpoint checks only that the process is up, not that it can serve
Health checks are skipped for instances that have been running over an hour
The 500s must come from the load balancer itself, not from the instances
questions.why: A shallow liveness check keeps passing while every real request fails. Add a readiness check that exercises critical dependencies (with care not to cascade), and alert on the 5xx rate so symptoms are caught even when checks pass.
questions.asked: Probes the difference between liveness, readiness and actual user-facing health.

questions.q: You mistakenly deployed a `301` redirect from `/pricing` to `/plans`, then removed it an hour later. Some users are still sent to `/plans`. Why?
choices: The CDN keeps every redirect rule for exactly 24 hours after it has been removed
The server still has the rule cached in memory until it is restarted
DNS resolvers cached the redirect along with the domain's A record
Browsers may cache a 301 indefinitely, so they redirect without asking again
questions.why: A 301 is 'moved permanently', and browsers cache it heuristically, often with no expiry, so they never re-request `/pricing`. Use 302 or 307 while testing, add explicit `Cache-Control` to permanent redirects, and treat a 301 as hard to undo.
questions.asked: A real 'I cannot undo it' incident; strong answers know 301 caching is sticky.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core 8 app using cookie authentication, an expired session makes `fetch('/api/orders')` return 200 with the login page's HTML. Why?
choices: Cookie auth redirects unauthenticated requests with 302, and fetch follows it
The API returned the login page deliberately as a fallback for any error
The browser converts every 401 response into the login page for security reasons
The session cookie was sent, but the API only accepts header tokens
questions.why: The cookie handler's default challenge is a redirect to the login path, which fetch follows transparently, ending at an HTML 200. For API paths, override `OnRedirectToLogin`/`OnRedirectToAccessDenied` to return 401/403 (.NET 10 does this for known API endpoints).
questions.asked: A classic mixed MVC-plus-API bug; knowing the redirect events shows real ASP.NET Core experience.

questions.q: During every rolling deploy to Kubernetes, users see a burst of errors for 20 seconds while new pods start. The pods have no readiness probe. Why?
choices: Pods get traffic once their containers start, even if the app is not ready yet
Rolling deploys always stop every old pod before starting the first new one
Pods without a readiness probe are restarted every 20 seconds by the kubelet
The service's DNS name changes during each deploy, so clients fail to resolve
questions.why: Without a readiness probe, a pod counts as ready once its containers run, so requests arrive before the app has bound its port or warmed up. A readiness probe on a real endpoint (and graceful shutdown for old pods) makes rolling deploys seamless.
questions.asked: Complements the liveness question; interviewers want the difference between the probe types.

questions.q: After importing 10,000 rows with explicit ids into a Postgres table with an identity column, new inserts fail with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint`. Why?
choices: The import disabled the primary key, and it must be recreated by hand
Postgres allows only one import per table, so later inserts are rejected
Explicit ids do not advance the sequence, so it hands out ids already used
The imported rows are still locked, so their ids are reported as duplicates
questions.why: Identity and serial columns draw from a sequence, which only moves when it generates a value. After a bulk load with explicit ids, reset it with `setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('t', 'id'), (SELECT max(id) FROM t))`.
questions.asked: A common data-migration bug; knowing `setval` shows hands-on Postgres experience.

questions.q: Your load test showed 50 ms responses at 2,000 requests per second, but production struggles at 300. The test hit the same ten product ids repeatedly. What went wrong?
choices: Load tests always overstate capacity by about seven times, so divide the result
The test's traffic was so repetitive that caches served nearly everything
Production uses HTTPS, which costs six times more CPU than the test's HTTP
The load test tool reported averages, whereas production reports medians
questions.why: Ten hot ids stay in every cache (application, database buffer pool, CDN), so the test measured cache hits. Realistic tests use production-like data volume and key distribution, including cold paths and writes.
questions.asked: Tests scepticism about benchmarks; strong answers design tests with realistic data.

questions.q: An EF Core app on Postgres works, but a raw SQL report `SELECT * FROM users` fails with `relation "users" does not exist`. The DbSet is `Users`. Why?
choices: Raw SQL cannot read tables that EF Core created through migrations
The table lives in a separate schema that raw queries cannot access
Postgres requires `SELECT *` to be written as `SELECT ALL` for tables
EF Core created the table as quoted `"Users"`, and quoted names are case-sensitive
questions.why: Postgres folds unquoted names to lowercase, but Npgsql quotes the names EF Core generates, so the table is literally `Users`. Quote it in raw SQL, or adopt snake_case naming (`UseSnakeCaseNamingConvention`) so both sides agree.
questions.asked: A common EF Core plus Postgres surprise; the naming-convention fix is the strong answer.

questions.q: Under load, users of an ASP.NET Core API occasionally see another user's name in responses. A `CurrentUserService` stores the user in a property set by middleware. What is the likely bug?
choices: The JWT library caches tokens and returns the most recently validated one
Kestrel reuses `HttpContext` objects, so the user claims leak between separate requests
The service is registered as a singleton, so concurrent requests overwrite it
The database returns rows for the wrong user when the pool is under pressure
questions.why: One singleton instance is shared by every request, so per-request state stored on it races. Register it as scoped, or read the user from `IHttpContextAccessor` each time; the Node equivalent is a module-level variable instead of AsyncLocalStorage.
questions.asked: Lifetimes bugs with security impact are exactly what interviewers probe in DI questions.

questions.q: The SPA works at the domain root, but deployed under `/app/` it shows a blank page and `Failed to load module script: ... MIME type of "text/html"`. What is wrong?
choices: The server sends the JavaScript with the wrong charset, which browsers reject for modules
The build assumes base `/`, so asset URLs miss and the fallback returns `index.html`
Module scripts cannot be served from subfolders on any static host
The browser blocks modules from paths that contain a trailing slash
questions.why: Assets are requested at `/assets/...` rather than `/app/assets/...`; the host's SPA fallback returns `index.html` for the unknown path, which the browser refuses as a module. Set the bundler's base path (Vite `base: '/app/'`) and the router's basename.
questions.asked: Base-path bugs are common when apps move behind a path prefix; reading the MIME error correctly is the key.

questions.q: After moving static assets to a CDN domain, icons from a web font show as empty boxes, while images and CSS load fine. What is missing?
choices: CORS headers on the font responses, since cross-origin fonts require them
A longer cache lifetime, since the fonts expire before the CSS is able to use them
A `preload` hint, since fonts are never downloaded without one
HTTP/2 on the CDN, since font files cannot be served over HTTP/1.1
questions.why: Browsers fetch `@font-face` files in CORS mode, so a font from another origin needs `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`; images and stylesheets have no such requirement. The console shows the blocked request.
questions.asked: A classic CDN migration bug; knowing fonts are special-cased under CORS is the insight.

questions.q: A dashboard's WebSocket connection drops every 60 seconds when no messages are sent, but stays up during busy periods. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The browser closes WebSockets that have been open for exactly one minute
The server's garbage collector closes sockets that have not been used recently
An idle timeout in a proxy or load balancer closes quiet connections
WebSockets have a protocol limit of 60 seconds without a message frame
questions.why: Load balancers and proxies drop connections with no traffic after their idle timeout. Send application or protocol-level pings (heartbeats) more often than the timeout, raise the timeout, and reconnect with backoff on the client.
questions.asked: Long-lived connections meet infrastructure timeouts; heartbeats plus reconnect is the expected answer.

questions.q: PDF generation with a headless browser works on your laptop but fails in the slim production container with errors about missing shared libraries. What is the fix?
choices: Run the container as root, since shared libraries require root to load
Increase the container's memory, since missing libraries mean memory pressure
Install the libraries at runtime with a startup script on every request
Use a base image that includes the browser's system dependencies and fonts
questions.why: Headless Chromium needs system libraries and fonts that slim images omit; your laptop already has them. Use the tool's documented image (for example the Playwright base image) or install the listed packages in the Dockerfile, not at runtime.
questions.asked: Environment parity again; the strong answer bakes dependencies into the image.

questions.q: An admin creates product 42, but `GET /products/42` keeps returning 404 for ten minutes. The API caches lookups for ten minutes. What happened?
choices: The database write is delayed by ten minutes so that inserts can be batched together
Someone requested it before creation, and the 'not found' result was cached
The CDN rejects new ids until it has seen them at least ten times
The API returns 404 for new products until the next deploy restarts it
questions.why: Caching a miss (negative caching) is useful against repeated lookups for absent keys, but it must have a short TTL and be invalidated on create. Here the earlier miss shadowed the new row for the full TTL.
questions.asked: Tests careful thinking about what a cache stores, including absence.

questions.q: A Node script updates 10,000 rows with `await Promise.all(rows.map(r => pool.query(sql, [r.id])))`. The pool has `max: 10`. It is slow and sometimes errors with connection timeouts. Why?
choices: `Promise.all` runs the queries one at a time, so it is always slow
All 10,000 queries are queued at once for ten connections, so waiters time out
Postgres rejects more than ten parameterised queries per second from any one client
`pool.query` cannot be used inside `map`, since it needs a callback
questions.why: Every query is started immediately, so thousands wait for a connection and some exceed the pool's acquire timeout. Bound the concurrency (a small limiter), or better, do the work in one set-based statement such as `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ANY($1)`.
questions.asked: Unbounded concurrency is a common Node mistake; strong answers prefer a single set-based query.

questions.q: An EF Core endpoint takes seconds and uses lots of memory. The code is `db.Orders.ToList().Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)`. What is wrong?
choices: `Where` after `ToList` is translated into a slower SQL subquery by EF Core
`ToList` disables indexes on the table for the rest of the request
The lambda captures `id`, which forces EF Core to recompile the query each time
`ToList()` loads the whole table into memory before filtering in C#
questions.why: Once `ToList()` runs, the query has executed; `Where` then filters in memory over every order. Keep the query as `IQueryable` until the end, `db.Orders.Where(...).ToList()`, so the filter becomes SQL.
questions.asked: The IQueryable versus IEnumerable boundary is a core EF Core concept, seen here as a bug.

questions.q: A dashboard shows the total order count with `SELECT count(*) FROM orders` on a 200-million-row Postgres table, and the page takes 20 seconds. What is a reasonable fix?
choices: Add an index on `id`, which lets Postgres return the count instantly
Switch to `count(id)`, which Postgres reads directly from the table header
Show an estimate from the planner's statistics, or maintain a counter
Run `VACUUM FULL` before each count so that the table is smaller
questions.why: Because of MVCC, Postgres must check row visibility, so an exact count scans the table or an index. Dashboards rarely need exactness: use `reltuples` from `pg_class`, a cached figure, or a counter table updated by the app or a trigger.
questions.asked: Shows you know exact counts are expensive in MVCC databases, and that 'approximately' is often fine.

questions.q: During a rolling deploy, some users get 404s from a new endpoint for a few minutes, then everything works. The frontend and backend deploy together. Why?
choices: New frontend code reached users while some requests still hit old API instances
The CDN rejects requests to new endpoints until their first cache miss
The API's router rebuilds its route table only after every instance is updated
The browser caches 404 responses for new URLs until the page is reloaded
questions.why: During a rollout, old and new versions serve side by side. Deploy the backend first and keep it backward-compatible, then release the frontend (or put the feature behind a flag) so no client calls an endpoint that might not exist yet.
questions.asked: Mixed-version windows are inherent in rolling deploys; the ordering answer shows real release experience.

questions.q: Some long-time users suddenly get `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` (or an Nginx 400 'Request Header Or Cookie Too Large') on every page. New users are fine. What is the likely cause?
choices: Their browsers send a newer HTTP version that the server does not support
Their accounts have too many roles for the server to process in time
Cookies have accumulated on your domain until the headers exceed the limit
Their IP addresses have been added to a blocklist by the web application firewall
questions.why: Large or numerous cookies (chunked auth cookies, analytics, per-feature cookies) ride along on every request and can exceed server header limits. Shrink them (store sessions server-side, drop unused cookies) rather than only raising the limit.
questions.asked: A real, confusing error; knowing that cookies are headers is the key insight.

questions.q: API latency rises whenever your hosted log platform is slow. The app sends each log entry to it over HTTP inside the request. What is the fix?
choices: Log less information per request, so each HTTP call to the platform is smaller
Take log shipping off the request path: batch it, or log to stdout for an agent
Raise the HTTP timeout for logging calls, so they fail less often under load
Switch logs to `debug` level in production, which bypasses the log platform
questions.why: Synchronous remote logging makes every request depend on the log service's latency. Asynchronous, batching sinks or writing to stdout and letting a collector ship logs decouples them, with bounded buffers to protect memory.
questions.asked: Observability should not hurt availability; interviewers like 'stdout plus a collector'.

questions.q: A Postgres login query uses `WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER(@e)`, and database CPU jumped after you added it. An index exists on `email`. Why?
choices: `LOWER` is not available in Postgres, so the driver emulates the query on the client side
The function call on the column prevents use of the plain index, forcing a scan
Lowercasing both sides doubles the rows returned, which doubles the CPU
Indexes on text columns are disabled whenever parameters are lowercased
questions.why: An index on `email` stores original values, so filtering on `LOWER(email)` cannot seek it. Create an expression index on `LOWER(email)`, use `citext`, or store emails normalised to lowercase.
questions.asked: Sargability comes up in every SQL performance conversation; the expression index is the strong answer.

questions.q: A .NET API compares roles with `role.ToUpper() == "ADMIN"`. It works everywhere except on servers configured with Turkish culture, where admins are denied. Why?
choices: Turkish culture uppercases `i` to `İ`, so `admin` becomes `ADMİN`
Turkish Windows servers cannot store strings in uppercase letters at all
`ToUpper` throws on non-English servers, so the comparison fails
The JWT library translates role names into the server's language
questions.why: Culture-sensitive casing maps `i` to dotted capital `İ` in Turkish. Compare identifiers with `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` or use `ToUpperInvariant`; culture rules are for text shown to people.
questions.asked: The famous 'Turkish I' problem; it tests awareness of culture-sensitive string operations.

questions.q: In the cloud, the first database query after several quiet minutes fails with 'connection reset' or hangs, then everything is fine. The pool keeps idle connections open for 30 minutes. What is a likely cause?
choices: The database restarts itself after a few quiet minutes to save resources
The driver closes idle connections, but the pool still hands them out
Queries after idle periods are rejected until the database's query cache has been refilled
A NAT or firewall silently drops idle TCP flows, so pooled connections are dead
questions.why: Cloud NAT gateways, load balancers and firewalls expire idle flows after a few minutes without telling either end. Set the pool's idle timeout below that limit, enable TCP keepalives, or validate connections on checkout.
questions.asked: A subtle infrastructure-meets-pooling bug; knowing it signals real cloud operations experience.

questions.q: A monthly report runs several `SELECT` statements under Postgres's default READ COMMITTED isolation. The totals section and the detail section sometimes disagree. Why?
choices: READ COMMITTED allows dirty reads, so uncommitted rows appear in one section
Each statement takes a new snapshot, so writes between them show up in only one section
Postgres caches the first statement's results and reuses them for the rest
Aggregates such as `SUM` are computed on a replica that lags behind
questions.why: Under READ COMMITTED every statement takes a fresh snapshot, so rows committed between the totals query and the detail query appear in only one. Run the report in a REPEATABLE READ (snapshot) transaction so all statements see the same data.
questions.asked: Isolation levels made concrete; strong answers pick snapshot isolation for multi-statement reads.

questions.q: A mobile app retries failed calls 3 times, the API gateway retries 3 times, and the API retries its database call 3 times. The database has a brief slowdown. What happens?
choices: Retries cancel each other out, so the database sees normal load
Only the outermost retries run, since the inner ones are disabled automatically by the SDK
Each failure can fan out into up to 27 database calls, amplifying the overload
The gateway detects the loop and stops all retries after the first failure
questions.why: Retries at every layer multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 attempts reach the bottom for one user action, turning a slowdown into an outage. Retry at one layer (usually closest to the failure), use retry budgets, and add backoff and circuit breakers.
questions.asked: Retry amplification is a classic resilience lesson; interviewers like the multiplication.

questions.q: A Node service's p99 latency spikes and CPU climbs in the hours before it is OOM-killed, while request volume is flat. What is happening in V8?
choices: The heap is near its limit, so V8 runs frequent full GCs that reclaim little
V8 recompiles every function when memory is low, which costs CPU time
The event loop switches to a slower mode once heap usage passes half
Node throttles incoming requests to protect its memory, which raises the tail latency
questions.why: As live objects approach `--max-old-space-size`, V8 runs mark-compact collections more and more often, each pausing the thread while freeing little. The latency and CPU rise are symptoms of the leak; fix the retention rather than just raising the limit.
questions.asked: Connects GC behaviour to user-visible latency, a sign of deep runtime understanding.

questions.q: A job takes a Redis lock with a 30-second TTL, but sometimes runs for 45 seconds. Occasionally two workers process the same batch. What is the core problem?
choices: Redis drops locks at random under memory pressure, whatever the TTL is
Two workers can never hold the same key, so the duplicate must come from retries
The TTL is measured in milliseconds, so the lock lasts only 30 ms
The lock expires while the first worker is still running, so a second takes it
questions.why: A lease with a TTL shorter than the work lets another worker acquire it mid-job. Extend the lease while working, check a fencing token when writing results, and keep processing idempotent, since no distributed lock is perfectly safe.
questions.asked: Distributed locks are subtle; strong answers mention fencing tokens and idempotency.

questions.q: A .NET API in Kubernetes has a CPU limit of 500m. Average CPU usage looks low, yet latency spikes periodically. What is a likely cause?
choices: Low CPU usage means the pod is idle, so the spikes must come from the network
The CPU limit is enforced as a quota per period, and bursts get throttled
Kubernetes pauses pods with CPU limits every minute to rebalance the nodes
The runtime ignores CPU limits and uses every core, which causes contention
questions.why: CPU limits use CFS quotas: a multi-threaded runtime can burn its 50 ms per 100 ms period in a burst and is then throttled for the rest of it, adding latency. Check the throttling metrics, and raise or remove limits while keeping requests.
questions.asked: CPU throttling is a well-known Kubernetes trap; averages hide it, which is the insight.

questions.q: A long-running .NET service's memory grows, and a dump shows thousands of `ReportViewModel` instances retained through a static `SettingsChanged` event. Why are they not collected?
choices: Static classes pin every object that was created while their static constructor was running
Events keep objects alive only in Debug builds, so the dump is misleading
The static event's delegate list references each subscriber, keeping it alive
The GC skips objects that implement `INotifyPropertyChanged` by design
questions.why: Subscribing an instance method to an event stores a reference to the instance in the publisher's delegate list; a static publisher lives forever, so subscribers never become unreachable. Unsubscribe (for example in `Dispose`) or use a weak-event pattern.
questions.asked: The classic .NET event-handler leak; reading a retention path in a dump is the practical skill.

questions.q: A colleague on another network says your site is down, but it loads fine for you. What is a sensible first check?
choices: Tell them to restart their laptop, since the site is clearly up for everyone
Test from outside your network, such as an external uptime checker or a phone on mobile data
Restart the production servers, since some users being affected means an outage
Clear the CDN cache, since partial outages are always caused by stale edge content
questions.why: 'Works for me' may be your cache, your DNS resolver or your office network. Checking from independent vantage points shows whether the problem is regional, DNS-related or specific to their network before anyone restarts anything.
questions.asked: Tests whether you verify scope before acting, a habit interviewers value.
